sections.title: I-A · Evaluate Data in the Patient Record

q.q: On a sputum culture report for a patient with suspected bacterial pneumonia, growth of at least what colony count of a respiratory pathogen is considered positive?
o: ≥ 10⁶ CFU/mL
≥ 10² CFU/mL
≥ 10³ CFU/mL
≥ 10⁴ CFU/mL
q.e: Samples that grow ≥ 10⁶ colony-forming units (CFU) per milliliter of a respiratory pathogen are considered positive for bacterial pneumonia. Inadequate collection methods or recent antibiotic administration can cause false-positive and false-negative results. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 1176–1181)
q.src: Sputum culture

q.q: A 54-year-old patient's chart shows an Epworth Sleepiness Scale score of 14 and a polysomnogram report with an apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) of 22/h. How should the respiratory therapist classify this patient's sleep apnea?
o: Moderate sleep apnea
Mild sleep apnea
Severe sleep apnea
Normal sleep study
q.e: Sleep apnea severity is judged by the frequency of AHI or RDI events per hour: 0–4/h is normal, 5–14/h is mild, 15–30/h is moderate, and > 30/h is severe. An AHI of 22/h falls in the moderate sleep apnea range, and an Epworth Sleepiness Scale score above the threshold value of 10 indicates excessive daytime sleepiness. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 1728–1732, 1794–1802)
q.src: Sleep study results

q.q: A 64-year-old patient with dyspnea has an echocardiogram showing increased left ventricular end-diastolic volume, increased left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35%. These findings are most consistent with:
o: Systolic heart failure
Diastolic heart failure
Pulmonary arterial hypertension
Cor pulmonale with right heart failure
q.e: Systolic heart failure (decreased LV contractility) is characterized on echocardiography by increased LV end-diastolic volume, increased LV end-diastolic pressure, and a decreased LV ejection fraction (< 45%). In diastolic failure, LV end-diastolic volume is normal or decreased and the LV ejection fraction is normal (> 50%). (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 2526–2541)
q.src: Echocardiography and ICP trends

sections.title: I-B · Perform Clinical Assessment

q.q: Which method should the respiratory therapist use to evaluate a change in a patient's skill level after demonstrating a respiratory care procedure?
o: Return demonstration
Teach-back
Written questionnaire
Family discussion
q.e: To evaluate a patient's skill level, use a return demonstration by asking the patient to perform the procedure after you have demonstrated it. Teach-back is used to evaluate patient knowledge, whereas discussion with the patient and family or observation of behavioral change evaluates attitudes. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 3204–3218)
q.src: Evaluation of patient learning

q.q: On a chest radiograph of a patient with a pneumothorax, where is a thoracostomy (chest) tube normally positioned to evacuate air?
o: Anterosuperiorly
Posteroinferiorly
Between T2 and T4
In the superior vena cava
q.e: To evacuate air in a pneumothorax, a thoracostomy tube is normally positioned anterosuperiorly, whereas to evacuate fluid it is positioned posteroinferiorly. Between T2 and T4 is the proper position for an endotracheal tube tip, and the superior vena cava is the target for a central venous catheter. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 4218–4227)
q.src: Chest radiograph evaluation

q.q: During an interview, a 38-year-old patient reports smoking 1.5 packs of cigarettes per day for 20 years and having the first cigarette immediately upon waking up. How should the respiratory therapist document this smoking history?
o: 30 pack-years with heavy nicotine dependence
13 pack-years with mild nicotine dependence
20 pack-years with moderate nicotine dependence
30 pack-years with minimal nicotine dependence
q.e: Multiplying 1.5 packs per day by 20 years equals 30 pack-years. Patients who smoke more than one pack a day and those who must have their first cigarette upon waking up are heavily nicotine dependent. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 2968–2980)
q.src: Smoking history

q.q: During an outpatient evaluation, a 66-year-old patient with COPD reports having to stop for breath after walking about 100 yards on level ground and answers 'yes' to 2 of the 6 basic Activities of Daily Living questions. How should the respiratory therapist classify the patient's breathlessness and ADL function?
o: Grade 3 (severe) breathlessness and severe ADL impairment
Grade 2 (moderate) breathlessness and moderate ADL impairment
Grade 4 (very severe) breathlessness and severe ADL impairment
Grade 3 (severe) breathlessness and moderate ADL impairment
q.e: On the ATS Breathlessness Scale, stopping for breath after walking about 100 yards or after a few minutes on level ground is Grade 3 (severe). On the 6-item basic ADL scale, a score of 6 indicates full function, 4 indicates moderate impairment, and 2 or less indicates severe impairment. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 2912–2929, 3039–3044)
q.src: Activities of daily living and breathlessness

q.q: Upon admission, a patient does not speak English and leaves an educational pamphlet upside down while identifying home inhalers only by their color. Which action should the respiratory therapist take FIRST to conduct the assessment?
o: Request a certified medical translator to interview the patient directly
Ask an adult family member at the bedside to interpret the questions
Provide detailed written instructions in the patient's native language
Postpone the interview until the patient learns basic medical terms
q.e: When a language barrier is present, you should request a certified medical translator to interview the patient; using family members is strongly discouraged due to privacy concerns unless it is an emergency. Leaving reading materials upside down and identifying medications by color rather than by name also indicate health literacy problems, so written pamphlets alone would be ineffective. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 3058–3083)
q.src: Learning needs and language barriers

q.q: A newborn has a composite Ballard Gestational Age score of 8, cold extremities, acrocyanosis, and a capillary refill time of 4 seconds. Which interpretation is most accurate?
o: Significant prematurity (≤ 28 weeks) with poor peripheral perfusion
Full-term gestation (38–42 weeks) with normal newborn acrocyanosis
Post-term gestation (> 42 weeks) with central arterial hypoxemia
Moderate prematurity (34–36 weeks) with adequate cardiac output
q.e: On the Ballard assessment, a composite score of 10 or less indicates significant prematurity (≤ 28 weeks' gestation), whereas a full-term infant (38–42 weeks) scores 35–45. Cold extremities, peripheral cyanosis (acrocyanosis), and a slow capillary refill taking 3 seconds or longer indicate reduced cardiac output and poor perfusion. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 3590–3594, 3799–3818, 4293–4294)
q.src: Ballard gestational age and capillary refill

sections.title: I-C · Perform Procedures to Gather Clinical Information

q.q: When using a point-of-care analyzer such as the i-STAT for arterial blood gas testing, within what maximum time after collection must the unchilled blood sample be analyzed?
o: Within 3 minutes
Within 15 minutes
Within 30 minutes
Within 60 minutes
q.e: For point-of-care cartridge testing on an instrument such as the i-STAT, you obtain the sample as usual, do not place it in ice, and analyze it within 3 minutes. A room-temperature sample in a plastic syringe for laboratory analysis must be run in under 30 minutes. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 4951–4966, 4924–4926)
q.src: Point-of-care blood gas analysis

q.q: A spontaneous breathing patient with a predicted body weight of 125 lb (57 kg) has a respiratory rate of 15/min and a tidal volume of 400 mL. What is this patient's alveolar minute ventilation?
o: 4.125 L/min
6.000 L/min
5.145 L/min
1.875 L/min
q.e: Unless otherwise indicated, assume physiologic deadspace (VD) is 1 mL per pound of predicted body weight (125 mL). Alveolar minute ventilation equals f × (VT − VD) = 15 × (400 mL − 125 mL) = 15 × 275 mL = 4125 mL/min, or 4.125 L/min (total minute ventilation is 6.000 L/min and deadspace ventilation is 1.875 L/min). (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 4672–4702)
q.src: Alveolar minute ventilation calculation

q.q: Six minutes into an apnea test for brain death determination, a patient's SpO₂ drops to 82% for 45 seconds and the systolic blood pressure falls to 84 mm Hg. What should the respiratory therapist do?
o: Terminate the test, draw an ABG, and place the patient back on the ventilator
Increase the tracheal catheter oxygen flow to 15 L/min and continue to 10 minutes
Apply 10 cm H₂O of CPAP with 100% O₂ and extend the test to 15 minutes
Perform a recruitment maneuver and restart the 10-minute apnea timer
q.e: The apnea test must be terminated if spontaneous respiratory effort occurs, a serious ectopic heart rhythm arises, the SpO₂ falls below 85% for more than 30 seconds, or the systolic blood pressure decreases to less than 90 mm Hg. When terminating, draw repeat ABGs and place the patient back on the ventilator at original settings. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 5480–5497)
q.src: Apnea test procedure

q.q: During laboratory polysomnography CPAP titration for obstructive sleep apnea, a patient continues to have obstructive apneas at a CPAP setting of 16 cm H₂O and cannot tolerate higher CPAP pressures. Which adjustment should the respiratory therapist make?
o: Initiate a trial of BPAP starting at an EPAP of 4 cm H₂O and an IPAP of 8 cm H₂O
Increase the CPAP level in 2 cm H₂O steps to a maximum of 25 cm H₂O
Reduce the CPAP pressure to 4 cm H₂O and bleed in 2 L/min of supplemental O₂
Continue CPAP at 16 cm H₂O and switch from a nasal mask to a full face mask
q.e: If a patient cannot tolerate high CPAP pressures, if obstructive respiratory events continue at CPAP > 15 cm H₂O, or if central sleep apnea emerges during titration, consider a trial of BPAP starting at an EPAP of 4 cm H₂O and an IPAP of 8 cm H₂O. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 5554–5576)
q.src: Polysomnography CPAP/BPAP titration

q.q: While measuring functional residual capacity (FRC) by the open-circuit nitrogen washout method, the respiratory therapist observes a sudden spike in expired N₂ concentration in the middle of the 7-minute test. This finding indicates:
o: A system or patient leak that invalidates the test
Severe bullous emphysema requiring a 15-minute washout
Completion of washout with alveolar N₂ below 1.0%
Depletion of the soda lime CO₂ absorber in the circuit
q.e: During open-circuit nitrogen washout, test validity depends on starting at FRC and an absence of leaks; an increased % N₂ in the middle of the test indicates a leak. Soda lime is used in the closed-circuit helium dilution method, not in open-circuit nitrogen washout. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 6146–6175)
q.src: Lung volume and DLCO testing

sections.title: I-D · Evaluate Procedure Results

q.q: On a normal capnogram, a rise above zero in the expired CO₂ waveform baseline during inspiration (Phase D to E) indicates:
o: An increase in mechanical deadspace causing rebreathing
An acute pulmonary embolism increasing alveolar deadspace
Sudden hyperventilation with washout of alveolar CO₂
Lack of an alveolar plateau from expiratory obstruction
q.e: During inhalation of fresh gas (D to E), the CO₂ concentration normally drops to zero; a rise in the expired CO₂ waveform baseline indicates an increase in mechanical deadspace (rebreathing). Lack of a clear alveolar plateau occurs in COPD, CHF, auto-PEEP, V/Q mismatch, and pulmonary emboli. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 6671–6675, 7917–7921)
q.src: Capnography waveform

q.q: During a sleep study, CPAP titration is classified as providing 'optimal' control when rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is not continually interrupted by arousals and the respiratory disturbance index (RDI) is reduced to:
o: Less than 5
10 or less
50% of baseline
75% of baseline
q.e: Control during CPAP/BPAP titration is classified as optimal when the titrated CPAP level reduces the RDI to less than 5 and REM sleep is not continually interrupted by arousals. Good control reduces the RDI to 10 or less (or by 50% if baseline RDI was < 15), and adequate control reduces an RDI above 10 by 75% from baseline. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 7650–7663)
q.src: CPAP titration evaluation

q.q: A patient with a body surface area of 2.0 m² has a cardiac output of 4.0 L/min and a heart rate of 100/min. What are the patient's stroke volume (SV) and cardiac index (CI), and how should they be interpreted?
o: SV 40 mL/beat and CI 2.0 L/min/m² — both are below normal limits
SV 40 mL/beat and CI 2.0 L/min/m² — both are within normal limits
SV 80 mL/beat and CI 4.0 L/min/m² — both are within normal limits
SV 25 mL/beat and CI 8.0 L/min/m² — SV is low and CI is elevated
q.e: Stroke volume equals CO (mL/min) ÷ HR = 4000 ÷ 100 = 40 mL/beat (normal 60–130 mL/beat), and cardiac index equals CO ÷ BSA = 4.0 ÷ 2.0 = 2.0 L/min/m² (normal 2.5–4.0 L/min/m²). Both values are below normal, which is associated with decreased cardiac contractility or increased afterload. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 7257–7268, 7330–7353)
q.src: Hemodynamic calculations

q.q: Over a 4-hour period, an adult receiving volume-control ventilation on a constant tidal volume of 500 mL and PEEP of 5 cm H₂O has the following pressures: PIP rises from 30 to 45 cm H₂O while Pplat remains 25 cm H₂O. Which change has occurred?
o: Airway resistance has increased while static compliance is unchanged
Static compliance has decreased while airway resistance is unchanged
Both static compliance and dynamic compliance have decreased equally
Alveolar plateau pressure has risen from acute pulmonary edema
q.e: Because Pplat − PEEP remains constant at 20 cm H₂O, static compliance (Crs) is unchanged at 25 mL/cm H₂O. Because the PIP − Pplat difference widens from 5 cm H₂O to 20 cm H₂O, airway resistance (Raw) is increasing due to a problem such as bronchospasm, excessive secretions, airway edema, or partial artificial airway occlusion. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 7420–7441, 7481–7490)
q.src: Pulmonary mechanics trend

q.q: A patient with severe COPD and a baseline PaCO₂ of 52 torr undergoes a 10-minute apnea test for brain death determination. No respiratory movements occur, the SpO₂ remains 96%, and the 10-minute ABG shows a PaCO₂ of 66 torr. How should the respiratory therapist interpret this test?
o: Inconclusive, because the PaCO₂ did not rise by > 20 torr above the chronic baseline
Positive for brain death, because the final PaCO₂ exceeded the 60-torr threshold
Invalid, because the SpO₂ remained above 85% throughout the 10-minute period
Negative for brain death, because COPD patients cannot undergo apnea testing
q.e: At the end of a 10-minute apnea study with absent respiratory movements, brain death is supported if the final PaCO₂ is at least 60 torr AND shows a > 20 torr increase from baseline for chronic CO₂ retainers. Because the PaCO₂ rose by only 14 torr (from 52 to 66 torr) and the patient remained stable without hypoxemia, the test may be repeated and extended to 12–15 minutes. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 5473–5475, 7690–7698)
q.src: Apnea test interpretation

q.q: A 62-year-old dyspneic patient has the following pulmonary function test results: FEV₁/FVC = 78%, FVC = 58% of predicted, TLC = 60% of predicted, and DLCO = 48% of predicted. These findings are most consistent with:
o: Restrictive lung disease due to interstitial lung disease (pulmonary fibrosis)
Restrictive disorder due to a chest wall deformity or neuromuscular weakness
Severe obstructive lung disease due to bullous pulmonary emphysema
Reversible obstructive airway disease due to chronic bronchial asthma
q.e: An FEV₁% (FEV₁/FVC) ≥ 70% with a low FVC and a low TLC (< 80% predicted) confirms a restrictive disorder. Among restrictive disorders, a low DLCO (< 50% of normal indicates a severe problem) points to interstitial lung disease such as pulmonary fibrosis, whereas chest wall or neuromuscular restriction has a normal or high DLCO. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 7847–7874)
q.src: Pulmonary function test interpretation

q.q: An ambulatory outpatient with suspected sleep-disordered breathing completes an in-home overnight pulse oximetry study that shows 19 desaturation events per hour (≥ 4% drop in SpO₂). Based on this result, which conclusion is appropriate?
o: Sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome is present; diagnostic PSG is not needed to confirm it
Sleep apnea is ruled out because fewer than 30 desaturation events per hour occurred
Full laboratory polysomnography is required before sleep apnea can be diagnosed
Nocturnal oxygen at 2 L/min should be started instead of positive airway pressure
q.e: On overnight oximetry, a desaturation event is a drop in SpO₂ of 4% or more, and an oxygen desaturation index (ODI) of 15 or more indicates the presence of sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (SAHS) without needing a follow-up diagnostic polysomnogram to confirm the diagnosis. Full diagnostic polysomnography is required when a suspected patient has fewer than 15 desaturation events per hour. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 7596–7606)
q.src: Overnight pulse oximetry

sections.title: I-E · Recommend Diagnostic Procedures

q.q: A 49-year-old patient with no prior cardiac history is admitted with unexplained generalized muscle weakness and new premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) on the bedside monitor. Which blood tests should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Electrolytes (potassium, calcium, magnesium), glucose, and thyroid-stimulating hormone
Cardiac biomarkers (CK-MB, troponin I), d-dimer, and ischemia-modified albumin
White blood cell count with differential, blood cultures, and arterial lactic acid
Prothrombin time (PT), International Normalized Ratio (INR), and platelet count
q.e: For patients with unexplained muscle weakness, recommend electrolytes (to assess for low potassium, calcium, and magnesium), glucose (for hypoglycemia), and thyroid-stimulating hormone (for hypothyroidism). For patients with PVCs or dysrhythmias without prior cardiac history, also recommend electrolytes (especially potassium and calcium) and thyroid-stimulating hormone. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 8210–8220)
q.src: Recommending laboratory tests

q.q: A 61-year-old patient with COPD has an awake room-air PaO₂ of 62 torr and PaCO₂ of 48 torr, but has developed polycythemia, pulmonary hypertension, morning headaches, and excessive daytime sleepiness. Which diagnostic study should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Overnight laboratory polysomnography
6-minute walk test with oximetry
Pre- and post-bronchodilator spirometry
Single-breath diffusing capacity (DLCO)
q.e: According to the AARC, laboratory polysomnography is specifically indicated for COPD patients whose awake PaO₂ is > 55 torr and whose condition is complicated by pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure, polycythemia, or excessive daytime sleepiness, as well as for patients with chronic hypoventilation (daytime PaCO₂ > 45 torr) and morning headaches. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 8810–8829)
q.src: Recommending sleep studies

q.q: A 58-year-old patient presents with severe dyspnea, tachypnea, SpO₂ of 86% on room air, dullness to percussion over the lower two-thirds of the right hemithorax, and a large right pleural effusion with mediastinal shift to the left on chest x-ray. Which procedure should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Therapeutic thoracentesis
Diagnostic bronchoscopy
Bronchoalveolar lavage
Ventilation/perfusion scan
q.e: You should recommend a therapeutic thoracentesis for any patient with a pleural effusion large enough to cause respiratory distress. A diagnostic thoracentesis is used to determine the cause of pleural fluid (transudative vs. exudative) or to obtain cytology samples. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 8915–8924, 9002–9004)
q.src: Recommending thoracentesis

q.q: A 67-year-old patient in the ICU has hypotension (BP 78/46 mm Hg), oliguria, bilateral fluffy infiltrates on portable chest x-ray, and refractory hypoxemia despite PEEP and vasoactive drug therapy, and the team cannot distinguish cardiogenic from noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. Which monitoring procedure should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Right-heart pulmonary artery catheterization
Central venous pressure monitoring alone
Modified Allen's test and radial artery puncture
Transthoracic ultrasound of the costophrenic angles
q.e: Pulmonary artery (PA) catheter monitoring is indicated to identify the cause of various shock states, identify the cause of pulmonary edema (by measuring PAWP to assess for left ventricular failure), assess the hemodynamic response to therapies, and optimize fluid and inotropic therapy. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 8881–8904, 7363–7379)
q.src: Recommending invasive hemodynamic monitoring

sections.title: II-A · Troubleshoot Devices During and After Assembling

q.q: When setting up a bubble CPAP system for an infant, what solution should the respiratory therapist add to the sterile water in the water seal for infection control?
o: 0.25% acetic acid
2% chlorhexidine
70% isopropyl alcohol
0.9% sodium chloride
q.e: For infant bubble CPAP systems, sterile water with 0.25% acetic acid is used in the water seal for infection control. Chlorhexidine and isopropyl alcohol are skin or surface disinfectants, and normal saline does not inhibit bacterial growth. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 9757–9765)
q.src: Bubble CPAP solution preparation

q.q: To avoid humidification problems in a mechanically ventilated patient with an artificial airway, gas delivered to the airway must carry a minimum water vapor content of:
o: 30 mg/L
10 mg/L
20 mg/L
44 mg/L
q.e: Gas delivered to a mechanically ventilated patient with an artificial airway must carry at least 30 mg/L of water vapor content to prevent humidification or temperature-regulation problems. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 9865–9871)
q.src: Airway humidification minimum water vapor content

q.q: Which of the following statements accurately describes the operating characteristics of a mechanical vane-type respirometer?
o: It tends to overread at high flows and underread at low flows
It tends to underread at high flows and overread at low flows
It is designed to measure forced expiratory flows during an FVC
It uses a heated wire to measure pressure changes across a screen
q.e: Like any turbine system, mechanical vane-type respirometers overread at high flows and underread at low flows, and they should never be used for forced vital capacity (FVC) maneuvers. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 11291–11302)
q.src: Mechanical vane respirometer characteristics

q.q: When monitoring an inhaled nitric oxide (INO) delivery system during mechanical ventilation, the analyzed nitrogen dioxide (NO2) concentration should not exceed:
o: 2–3 ppm
5–6 ppm
20 ppm
q.e: Nitrogen dioxide (NO2) is a toxic by-product formed when nitric oxide contacts oxygen, and analyzed NO2 levels should not exceed 2–3 ppm. An initial therapeutic INO dose is 20 ppm and is often reduced to 5–6 ppm. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 18818–18826, 18878–18885)
q.src: Inhaled nitric oxide toxic by-product limit

q.q: A home-care patient is receiving oxygen via nasal cannula at 2 L/min from a liquid oxygen (LOX) base reservoir that contains 50 lb of liquid oxygen. Approximately how many minutes will the reservoir last?
o: 8600 minutes
4300 minutes
17,200 minutes
21,500 minutes
q.e: At normal operating pressures, 1 lb of liquid oxygen equals approximately 344 L of gaseous oxygen, so 50 lb provides 50 × 344 = 17,200 L; dividing by 2 L/min yields 8600 minutes. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 9602–9608)
q.src: Liquid oxygen duration calculation

q.q: A patient with severe post-extubation stridor is ordered to receive a 70% helium/30% oxygen mixture via a nonrebreathing mask. If the mixture is delivered through a standard oxygen flowmeter set at 10 L/min, what is the actual heliox flow delivered to the patient?
o: 16 L/min
14 L/min
18 L/min
10 L/min
q.e: When delivering a 70/30 heliox mixture through an oxygen flowmeter, a correction factor of 1.6 is applied (10 L/min × 1.6 = 16 L/min). The factors 1.8 and 1.4 apply to 80/20 and 60/40 mixtures, respectively. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 11259–11264)
q.src: Heliox flowmeter correction calculation

q.q: A preterm neonate is receiving bubble CPAP with a set pressure of 5 cm H2O and a gas flow of 6 L/min, but the airway pressure manometer consistently reads 8 cm H2O while the water seal is bubbling vigorously. After verifying that the circuit tubing is free of condensate, what should the respiratory therapist do?
o: Raise the submersed expiratory limb or lower the water level in the seal
Lower the submersed expiratory limb or add sterile water to the chamber
Increase the continuous gas flowmeter setting from 6 L/min to 10 L/min
Apply a chin strap and switch the infant to larger binasal CPAP prongs
q.e: An airway pressure ≥ 2 cm H2O above the set CPAP level in a bubble CPAP system can be caused by excess water immersion; raising the submersed expiratory limb or lowering the water level to the prescribed CPAP pressure corrects the excessive pressure. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 9775–9795, 12069–12072)
q.src: Bubble CPAP excessive airway pressure troubleshooting

q.q: A mechanically ventilated adult is receiving humidification via a heated passover humidifier set to 37°C, and the low airway temperature alarm sounds at 31°C. The reservoir is full of warm water, ventilator flows are unchanged, and a room fan is blowing directly across the ventilator circuit. What should the respiratory therapist do?
o: Redirect the external fan or cover the circuit temperature probe with a cloth
Replace the heated passover humidifier unit with a heat and moisture exchanger
Drain the warm water from the humidifier reservoir and refill with cool water
Disconnect the patient circuit and allow the heater to warm up without gas flow
q.e: An external fan or air-conditioning vent blowing on the temperature probe can cause a low airway temperature reading on a heated passover humidifier, which is corrected by redirecting the fan or covering the probe with a cloth. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 9940–9954)
q.src: Heated passover humidifier low temperature alarm

q.q: A patient on mechanical ventilation is scheduled for an inhaled bronchodilator via an electronic nondisposable vibrating-mesh nebulizer. Thirty minutes into a treatment that normally finishes in 10 minutes, weak nebulization is observed and half of the medication remains in the cup despite a green AC power indicator light. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Clean or replace the nebulizer because the mesh plate is clogged with residual drug
Increase the ventilator bias flow to 10 L/min to push aerosol out of the chamber
Move the vibrating-mesh nebulizer from the humidifier inlet to the expiratory limb
Connect the nebulizer to a 50-psi oxygen source and set the flowmeter to 8 L/min
q.e: Weak nebulization, a longer than expected treatment time, and medication left in a nondisposable mesh nebulizer when the power source is functioning properly indicate that the mesh plate is clogged with residual drug and must be cleaned or replaced. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 10133–10151, 12085–12088)
q.src: Electronic vibrating-mesh nebulizer troubleshooting

q.q: A patient with COPD using a tiotropium soft-mist inhaler (Respimat) reports receiving very little mist during inhalation. You observe the patient rotate the clear base until it clicks, flip open the cap, wrap both hands tightly over the side air vents on the mouthpiece, and press the dose-release button while inhaling rapidly over 1 second. Which instruction should you give?
o: Avoid covering the air vents and take a slow, deep breath while pressing the button
Attach a valved holding chamber to the mouthpiece and inhale rapidly over 1 second
Keep the mouthpiece cap closed while rotating the base and actuating the dose button
Exhale forcefully into the mouthpiece before pressing the medication release button
q.e: When using a slow-mist inhaler (Respimat), the patient must seal their lips around the mouthpiece without covering the air vents and take a slow, deep breath while pressing the dose-release button; spacers and valved holding chambers cannot be used with this device. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 18593–18613)
q.src: Soft-mist inhaler (Respimat) patient technique

q.q: Before applying a self-inflating bag-valve-mask (BVM) resuscitator to an intubated patient, the respiratory therapist squeezes the bag to expel its gas and then occludes the patient connection port. The bag fails to reinflate while the patient port remains occluded. What is the cause of this finding, and what action should be taken?
o: The bag inlet valve is jammed or positioned incorrectly; replace the BVM
The pressure relief pop-off valve is stuck open; twist the cap to lock it
The oxygen input flowmeter is set below 15 L/min; increase the oxygen flow
The nonrebreathing patient valve is working normally; connect to the patient
q.e: When a BVM is squeezed and the patient connection is occluded, the bag should reinflate via the inlet valve; failure of this test indicates that the bag inlet valve is jammed or positioned incorrectly, and the BVM must be replaced. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 10240–10253)
q.src: Self-inflating BVM pre-use operational test

q.q: A mechanically ventilated patient with an 8.0-mm oral endotracheal tube has a cuff pressure that repeatedly drops from 25 cm H2O to 8 cm H2O within minutes, triggering low exhaled volume alarms. When 5 mL of air is injected into the pilot balloon, air is heard hissing from a small crack in the pilot inflation valve, while the pilot tubing itself is intact. What should the respiratory therapist do?
o: Attach a three-way stopcock to the valve outlet and reinflate the cuff to 20–30 cm H2O
Deflate the cuff completely and withdraw the endotracheal tube 2 cm toward the incisors
Clamp the endotracheal tube shaft with hemostats just above the level of the incisors
Remove the endotracheal tube immediately and ventilate the patient with a nasal mask
q.e: When a cuff leak is caused by a leaking one-way pilot valve or pilot tube, attaching a stopcock to the valve outlet (or inserting a small-gauge needle with a three-way stopcock into the pilot line) allows the cuff to be reinflated and avoids unnecessary reintubation. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 10862–10876, 15059–15066)
q.src: Endotracheal tube pilot line leak troubleshooting

q.q: A spontaneous-breathing patient with a size 8.0 cuffed tracheostomy tube has the cuff deflated and a one-way speaking valve placed on the hub. Within 1 minute, the patient develops severe respiratory distress, tachypnea of 34/min, SpO2 of 86%, and inability to exhale. What should the respiratory therapist do IMMEDIATELY?
o: Remove the speaking valve immediately and ensure all air is removed from the cuff
Inflate the tracheostomy tube cuff with 10 mL of air to seal the lower trachea
Attach a heat and moisture exchanger between the speaking valve and the tube hub
Instruct the patient to exhale forcefully through the tracheostomy tube lumen
q.e: A speaking valve is a one-way valve that allows inspiration through the tube but blocks expiration; if a patient experiences distress with the valve in place, the therapist must remove the valve immediately and ensure all air has been removed from the cuff. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 11058–11075, 15405–15409)
q.src: Speaking valve respiratory distress troubleshooting

q.q: Before suctioning an intubated adult, the respiratory therapist turns the wall vacuum regulator to continuous mode at −120 mm Hg and occludes the end of the connecting tubing. The gauge reads −120 mm Hg and all tubing and lid connections are tight, but no suction is felt at the catheter connection and the collection canister is filled to the top with secretions. What is the cause of this problem?
o: The full collection canister has closed the float shut-off valve, blocking vacuum
The wall vacuum pressure of −120 mm Hg is too low to generate flow in an adult
The suction catheter external diameter exceeds half the internal airway diameter
The regulator is operating in intermittent mode rather than continuous suction
q.e: Suction canisters incorporate a trap or float valve to prevent aspiration of fluids into the regulator; if the canister is full, the float valve closes and blocks vacuum from reaching the patient tubing. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 10746–10752, 11161–11171, 12164–12166)
q.src: Wall suction canister float valve troubleshooting

q.q: A patient with a right-sided chest tube attached to a wet three-chamber pleural drainage system at −20 cm H2O suction has continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber. When the respiratory therapist briefly pinches the chest tube near the patient's chest wall insertion site, the bubbling in the water-seal chamber continues. Where is the air leak located, and what should be done?
o: Between the patient and the drainage unit; tighten connections, seal tears, and prepare a new unit
Inside the patient’s pleural space from a bronchopleural fistula; increase suction to −30 cm H2O
At the chest wall insertion wound; apply a sterile petroleum jelly gauze pad around the chest tube
In the suction control chamber atmospheric vent; occlude the vent port with waterproof adhesive tape
q.e: If briefly pinching the chest tube near the insertion site does not stop continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber, the leak is between the patient and the collection system, which is managed by tightening connections, taping any tears temporarily, and preparing a new drainage unit. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 11708–11722)
q.src: Pleural drainage water-seal bubbling troubleshooting

q.q: A neonate in the NICU is being monitored with a transcutaneous blood gas monitor heated to 42°C. Over 2 minutes, the PtcCO2 drops abruptly from 44 torr to 2 torr while the PtcO2 rises from 65 torr to 148 torr, and the infant appears comfortable with stable vital signs and SpO2 of 95%. What is the most likely cause, and how should it be corrected?
o: Air is leaking around the sensor adhesive ring; reapply the sensor using a new adhesive ring
The neonate has developed an acute tension pneumothorax; prepare for needle decompression
The skin under the heated sensor has become vasoconstricted; increase sensor heat to 45°C
The arterial blood gas analyzer has a positive bias error; perform a two-point calibration
q.e: An air leak around the transcutaneous sensor adhesive ring causes a dramatic fall in PtcCO2 toward 0 torr and a rise in PtcO2 toward room air (~150 torr), which is corrected by reapplying the sensor with a new adhesive ring. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 11824–11829, 12207–12209)
q.src: Transcutaneous monitor adhesive ring leak

q.q: A spontaneously breathing patient receiving procedural sedation is being monitored with a sidestream capnograph via a nasal sampling cannula. The patient has regular chest wall excursion at 16 breaths/min and an SpO2 of 98%, but the PetCO2 display suddenly drops from 38 torr to 0 torr. What should the respiratory therapist do?
o: Check the sampling line for kinks, condensate occlusion, or disconnection and replace if needed
Turn off the body temperature, pressure, saturated (BTPS) correction setting on the capnograph
Disconnect the patient from the nasal cannula and initiate bag-valve-mask ventilation with 100% O2
Remove the mainstream sensor window from the airway adapter, wipe off sputum, and recalibrate
q.e: When a sidestream capnograph reading suddenly drops to 0 torr in a patient who is breathing normally, the sampling line is kinked, clogged with condensate, or disconnected, and should be unkinked, unclogged, or replaced. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 11860–11873, 12210–12212)
q.src: Sidestream capnograph zero reading troubleshooting

q.q: A physician is preparing to perform a laser bronchoscopy through an oral endotracheal tube on a mechanically ventilated patient currently receiving an FiO2 of 0.60 with an SpO2 of 99%. To minimize the risk of endobronchial ignition or airway fire before the laser is fired, what should the respiratory therapist do?
o: Reduce the FiO2 to below 0.40 if tolerated and ensure the laser tip is at least 5 mm from the scope
Increase the FiO2 to 1.00 for preoxygenation and wipe the laser tip clean with 70% isopropyl alcohol
Lubricate the outer sheath of the bronchoscope with petroleum jelly and remove the oral bite block
Advance the endotracheal tube tip to within 2 mm of the lesion so the laser fires inside the tube
q.e: To avoid endobronchial ignition or fire during laser bronchoscopy, the FiO2 should be kept below 0.40 if possible, alcohol must not be used on the laser tip, and the laser tip must be at least 5 mm away from the scope outlet and as far from the ETT as possible. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 11946–11950)
q.src: Laser bronchoscopy fire prevention

q.q: An ICU patient has a radial arterial catheter connected to a hemodynamic monitor. The arterial blood pressure reading changes from 118/72 mm Hg to 82/68 mm Hg with a flattened, damped pressure waveform, while a manual cuff blood pressure on the opposite arm is 120/74 mm Hg. Which action should the respiratory therapist take to resolve the damped waveform?
o: Aspirate any clot from the catheter with a syringe and flush the line with heparinized saline
Lower the pressure transducer 15 cm below the level of the fourth intercostal space at the axilla
Switch the monitor display scale from the high arterial pressure setting to a low venous setting
Remove the patient from positive end-expiratory pressure while recording the pressure reading
q.e: A damped arterial pressure waveform (reduced amplitude) is commonly caused by partial occlusion of the catheter tip by a clot or air bubbles in the system, which is corrected by aspirating the clot with a syringe and flushing with heparinized saline (or flushing out air bubbles). (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 5087–5115)
q.src: Arterial catheter damped waveform troubleshooting

sections.title: II-B · Ensure Infection Prevention or Control, Safety, and Performance of Quality Assurance Procedures

q.q: When processing heat-sensitive semicritical respiratory equipment in glutaraldehyde (Cidex) at room temperature, how long is required for high-level disinfection compared with true sterilization?
o: 20 minutes for high-level disinfection; 10 hours for sterilization
10 minutes for high-level disinfection; 30 minutes for sterilization
30 minutes for high-level disinfection; 2 hours for sterilization
1 hour for high-level disinfection; 24 hours for sterilization
q.e: With glutaraldehyde (Cidex) at room temperature, high-level disinfection is achieved in 20 minutes, whereas true sterilization requires a full 10 hours of immersion. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 12674–12683)
q.src: Glutaraldehyde disinfection vs sterilization exposure time

q.q: Pasteurization provides high-level disinfection for reusable semicritical respiratory care equipment by immersing the items in hot water at:
o: Greater than 158°F (70°C) for 30 minutes
Greater than 140°F (60°C) for 10 minutes
Greater than 120°F (49°C) for 20 minutes
Greater than 212°F (100°C) for 60 minutes
q.e: Pasteurization disinfects semicritical items via immersion in hot water at greater than 158°F (70°C) for 30 minutes. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 12727–12738)
q.src: Pasteurization temperature and duration

q.q: According to ATS/ERS quality control standards for a daily volumetric spirometer leak check, when a constant pressure of 3 cm H2O is applied for 1 minute, the volume loss must be:
o: No more than 10 mL/min
No more than 50 mL/min
No more than 100 mL/min
No more than 150 mL/min
q.e: During a daily leak check of a volumetric spirometer under 3 cm H2O constant pressure for 1 minute, the system should lose no more than 10 mL/min; larger losses indicate a leak that must be corrected before testing. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 13400–13414, 13426–13432)
q.src: Volumetric spirometer daily leak test standard

q.q: When performing quality control operational verification on a microprocessor-controlled mechanical ventilator, when should an extended self-test (EST) be performed?
o: Between each application of the ventilator on different patients
After internal preventative maintenance is completed every 6 months
Once daily while an intubated patient is connected to the circuit
Whenever switching between volume-control and pressure-control modes
q.e: An extended self-test (EST) includes the power-on-self-test (POST) plus comprehensive function checks and should be performed between each application of a ventilator on different patients. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 13560–13574)
q.src: Computerized ventilator extended self-test (EST) frequency

q.q: Before performing diagnostic spirometry, a respiratory therapist injects a 3.0-L calibration syringe into a computerized spirometer and obtains a measured volume of 3.31 L. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this calibration error, and how should it be corrected?
o: BTPS correction is turned ON; deactivate BTPS correction and repeat the 3.0-L calibration check
A leak is present in the spirometer breathing circuit; tighten the tubing connections and retest
The syringe plunger was pushed too rapidly; reinject the 3.0-L syringe over at least 12 seconds
The volume is within the acceptable ±3% ATS range; proceed with scheduled patient PFT testing
q.e: The acceptable ATS volume calibration range for a 3.0-L syringe (±3% or ±50 mL) is 2.91 to 3.09 L. A reading approximately 10% higher than 3.0 L (such as 3.31 L) occurs when BTPS correction is left ON during ambient syringe calibration; deactivating BTPS correction and rechecking zeroing resolves the high reading. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 13415–13425, 13460–13465)
q.src: Spirometer 3-L calibration syringe error troubleshooting

q.q: After drawing an arterial blood gas in a patient’s room, a container drops and spills approximately 30 mL of blood mixed with a contaminated needle onto the floor. After putting on gloves and appropriate PPE, how should the respiratory therapist manage the sharp and decontaminate the spill?
o: Pick up the needle with forceps, absorb visible blood, and disinfect with a 1:10 bleach dilution
Pick up the needle by hand, rinse the floor with water, and apply a 1:100 bleach dilution
Recap the needle using both hands, cover with a towel, and spray with 70% isopropyl alcohol
Sweep the needle into a red biohazard plastic bag and mop the spill with detergent and water
q.e: For a blood spill involving sharps and a larger volume (> 10 mL), you must wear PPE, pick up sharps with forceps to discard in a puncture-resistant container, clean visible blood with disposable absorbent material, and disinfect the area using a 1:10 dilution of sodium hypochlorite (1:100 is for small spills < 10 mL). (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 12835–12849)
q.src: Blood spill sodium hypochlorite dilution and sharps handling

sections.title: III-A · Maintain a Patent Airway Including the Care of Artificial Airways

q.q: When evaluating an adult chest radiograph to confirm proper endotracheal tube placement, at what distance above the carina should the tube tip be positioned?
o: 4 to 6 cm above the carina, between T2 and T4
1 to 2 cm above the carina, between T5 and T7
7 to 9 cm above the carina, at the C7 vertebra
2 to 3 cm above the carina, at the aortic arch
q.e: On a chest x-ray, the endotracheal tube tip should sit about 4 to 6 cm above the carina, which normally corresponds to the level between T2 and T4. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 14604–14609)
q.src: Endotracheal tube position on chest x-ray

q.q: A tracheostomy patient has the tube cuff fully deflated and a one-way speaking valve attached. Within 2 minutes, the patient develops acute respiratory distress with tachypnea and a drop in SpO2 from 97% to 88%. Which of the following should the respiratory therapist do FIRST?
o: Remove the one-way speaking valve immediately
Reinflate the tracheostomy cuff to 25 cm H2O
Pass a suction catheter through the speaking valve
Switch the oxygen delivery device to a T-tube
q.e: If a patient with a speaking valve and a deflated cuff develops respiratory distress due to upper airway obstruction, secretions, or an oversized tube, the speaking valve must be removed immediately. Inflating the cuff with a one-way valve in place would completely trap exhaled gas. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 14760–14774)
q.src: Speaking valve troubleshooting

q.q: A hospitalized post-laryngectomy patient with a double-cannula laryngectomy tube exhibits stridor, suprasternal retractions, and an SpO2 of 82%. After calling the rapid response team and removing the stoma filter and inner cannula, the respiratory therapist attempts to pass a suction catheter, but it cannot be advanced into the stoma. Which of the following should the therapist do NEXT?
o: Remove the laryngectomy tube and ventilate with a pediatric mask or LMA over the stoma
Attach a bag-valve-mask resuscitator directly to the outer laryngectomy cannula
Perform a head-tilt/chin-lift maneuver and ventilate via an adult oronasal mask
Instill 10 mL of sterile normal saline into the outer cannula and suction again
q.e: If a suction catheter cannot be passed through a laryngectomy tube after removing the inner cannula and accessories, the entire laryngectomy tube should be removed and bag-valve-mask ventilation with O2 provided via a pediatric face mask or LMA applied over the stoma. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 14733–14751)
q.src: Laryngectomy airway obstruction

q.q: A mechanically ventilated patient on volume control has a drop in exhaled tidal volume from 500 mL to 340 mL, decreased peak airway pressure, and audible gurgling at the mouth. Advancing the endotracheal tube slightly does not resolve the leak, and inspection reveals a small tear in the proximal pilot tube near the one-way inflation valve. Which of the following should the respiratory therapist do?
o: Insert a needle with a stopcock into the pilot tube distal to the leak and reinflate the cuff
Remove the endotracheal tube immediately and reintubate the patient by direct laryngoscopy
Attach a three-way stopcock directly to the outlet of the leaking one-way inflation valve
Maintain continuous air flow into the pilot balloon using a low-flow oxygen flowmeter
q.e: After ruling out partial extubation at the vocal cords, a leak located in the pilot tube can be bypassed by placing a needle with a stopcock into the pilot tube distal to the leak, allowing cuff reinflation without reintubation. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 15058–15081)
q.src: Tracheal tube cuff and pilot tube leaks

q.q: An intubated adult receiving volume-controlled ventilation with a heat and moisture exchanger (HME) has a core temperature of 31.5°C, a spontaneous minute volume of 12.4 L/min, and thick secretions that have required changing the HME five times in the past 24 hours. Which of the following should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Remove the HME and switch the patient to an active heated humidifier
Replace the current HME with a larger hygroscopic condenser filter
Switch the patient to an unheated passover humidifier in the circuit
Instill sterile normal saline into the tube before each HME change
q.e: HMEs are contraindicated in patients with thick secretions, hypothermia (body temperature < 32°C), or high spontaneous minute volumes (> 10 L/min), and whenever an HME must be changed more than four times per day; the patient should be switched to a heated humidifier. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 15176–15192)
q.src: Heat and moisture exchanger contraindications

q.q: An alert intubated patient completes a 60-minute spontaneous breathing trial with a respiratory rate of 18/min, SpO2 of 96% on FiO2 0.35, a strong cough on suctioning, and a maximum expiratory pressure (MEP) of 72 cm H2O. After suctioning above the cuff, deflating the cuff completely, and occluding the tube outlet, the therapist hears no air movement around the tube. Which of the following is the most appropriate action?
o: Withhold extubation and notify the physician of the absent cuff leak
Proceed with extubation and apply a cool bland aerosol mask immediately
Administer a neuromuscular blocking agent before removing the tube
Extubate the patient over an airway-exchange catheter connected to oxygen
q.e: Although the patient passed the SBT and has adequate cough strength (MEP > 60 cm H2O), the absence of airflow around the occluded tube with the cuff deflated indicates a negative cuff-leak test and a high risk for post-extubation upper airway obstruction. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 15312–15325)
q.src: Extubation readiness and cuff-leak test

sections.title: III-B · Perform Airway Clearance and Lung Expansion Techniques

q.q: When setting up a mechanical insufflation–exsufflation (cough-assist) device for a patient with neuromuscular weakness, which of the following inhalation and exhalation pressure ranges should the respiratory therapist select?
o: Inhalation pressure of 15 to 40 cm H2O and exhalation pressure of −35 to −45 cm H2O
Inhalation pressure of 5 to 15 cm H2O and exhalation pressure of −10 to −20 cm H2O
Inhalation pressure of 45 to 60 cm H2O and exhalation pressure of −60 to −80 cm H2O
Inhalation pressure of 20 to 30 cm H2O and exhalation pressure of −100 to −120 cm H2O
q.e: During mechanical insufflation–exsufflation, the inhalation pressure should be set between 15 and 40 cm H2O and the exhalation pressure between 35 and 45 cm H2O (negative pressure), using the lowest effective pressures. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 16073–16087)
q.src: Mechanical insufflation-exsufflation pressures

q.q: A patient with a severe traumatic brain injury is receiving mechanical ventilation and has coarse rhonchi in the bilateral lower lobes. Vital signs show HR 94/min, BP 126/78 mm Hg, SpO2 95%, and an intracranial pressure (ICP) of 24 mm Hg. An order is received for postural drainage, percussion, and vibration (PDPV) to the lower lobes. Which of the following should the respiratory therapist do?
o: Withhold postural drainage and contact the physician because ICP exceeds 20 mm Hg
Place the patient in a prone position with the foot of the bed elevated 18 inches
Perform postural drainage in a flat supine position and limit each position to 5 minutes
Preoxygenate with 100% oxygen and proceed with standard head-down postural drainage
q.e: An intracranial pressure (ICP) greater than 20 mm Hg is a contraindication to postural drainage, percussion, and vibration (PDPV), because positioning and chest manipulation can further elevate ICP. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 15589–15615, 16445–16448)
q.src: Postural drainage contraindications

q.q: A 74-year-old woman with severe osteoporosis and expiratory muscle weakness has a weak cough with a maximum expiratory pressure (MEP) of 42 cm H2O and retained airway secretions. Which of the following assisted cough techniques is CONTRAINDICATED for this patient?
o: Lateral chest compression (thoracic squeeze) over the lower rib cage
Abdominal thrust applied to the epigastric region during exhalation
Forced expiratory technique (huff cough) performed with an open glottis
Manually assisted inspiration using a modified bag-valve resuscitator
q.e: Lateral chest compression (thoracic squeeze) is contraindicated in patients with osteoporosis or flail chest due to the risk of rib fractures, whereas abdominal thrust is contraindicated in pregnant women. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 16145–16166)
q.src: Assisted cough contraindications

q.q: A patient with severe COPD in a pulmonary rehabilitation program is starting inspiratory muscle training (IMT) with a calibrated spring-loaded threshold resistor. The patient's baseline maximum inspiratory pressure (MIP) is −60 cm H2O. At what minimum initial inspiratory pressure load should the device be set once the patient is accustomed to breathing through it?
o: −18 cm H2O (30% of MIP)
−6 cm H2O (10% of MIP)
−30 cm H2O (50% of MIP)
−45 cm H2O (75% of MIP)
q.e: During inspiratory muscle training, resistance should be increased until the inspiratory pressure load is at least 30% of the patient's MIP (30% of −60 cm H2O = −18 cm H2O), and then increased by 5% per week as tolerated. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 16400–16427)
q.src: Inspiratory muscle training protocol

sections.title: III-C · Support Oxygenation and Ventilation

q.q: An adult patient is admitted with a large lung abscess in the right lower lobe and coarse purulent secretions. On a nasal cannula at 4 L/min, the patient's SpO2 is 89% and respiratory rate is 26/min. How should the respiratory therapist position this patient to optimize gas exchange and protect the airways?
o: Right lateral decubitus position with the left lung positioned up
Left lateral decubitus position with the left lung positioned down
Prone position with the abdomen freely suspended for 12 hours
Trendelenburg position with the foot of the bed elevated 18 inches
q.e: Although unilateral lung disease is usually managed with the good lung down, exceptions include a lung abscess or pulmonary bleeding, in which the good lung (left lung) must be kept in the upward position to prevent pus or blood from draining into the healthy lung. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 16646–16656)
q.src: Patient positioning for unilateral lung abscess

q.q: A 6-foot-tall (72-in.) male weighing 120 kg (265 lb) is intubated for acute hypercapnic respiratory failure secondary to an opioid overdose. When initiating volume-controlled assist/control ventilation at 8 mL/kg of predicted body weight (PBW), which of the following starting tidal volumes should the respiratory therapist select?
o: 625 mL
960 mL
350 mL
q.e: Initial tidal volume is based on 6 to 8 mL/kg of predicted body weight (PBW) rather than actual body weight to avoid excessive volumes; for a 6-foot (72-in.) male weighing 120 kg (265 lb), 8 mL/kg PBW yields a starting tidal volume of approximately 625 mL (in the 600–800 mL range), and not 1200 mL. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 16901–16904, 16943–16955)
q.src: Initial tidal volume by predicted body weight

q.q: An intubated adult with ARDS is receiving airway pressure release ventilation (APRV) with Phigh 26 cm H2O, Plow 4 cm H2O, Thigh 5.0 seconds, Tlow 0.5 seconds, and FiO2 0.50. Arterial blood gases reveal pH 7.26, PaCO2 58 torr, PaO2 76 torr, and HCO3− 25 mEq/L. Which of the following changes should the respiratory therapist recommend to correct the respiratory acidosis?
o: Decrease Thigh from 5.0 to 3.5 seconds to increase the release frequency
Increase Thigh from 5.0 to 6.5 seconds to reduce the release frequency
Increase Plow from 4 to 8 cm H2O while keeping Phigh at 26 cm H2O
Increase the FiO2 from 0.50 to 0.70 while keeping timing constant
q.e: During APRV, PaCO2 is decreased and pH is increased either by increasing the release frequency (shortening Thigh within the 3–5 second range) or by increasing ΔP (Phigh − Plow). Increasing Plow while keeping Phigh constant reduces ΔP and worsens hypercapnia. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 16955–16970, 17024–17027)
q.src: Adjusting airway pressure release ventilation

q.q: A 65-kg (PBW) patient with severe ARDS is ventilated in the VC, A/C mode at a set rate of 35/min, VT of 390 mL (6 mL/kg PBW), PEEP of 14 cm H2O, and FiO2 of 0.60. The plateau pressure is 32 cm H2O, and the ABG shows pH 7.26, PaCO2 56 torr, and PaO2 64 torr. Which of the following should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Decrease the set VT from 390 mL to 325 mL (5 mL/kg)
Maintain the current settings and allow permissive hypercapnia
Increase the set VT from 390 mL to 520 mL (8 mL/kg)
Increase the mandatory rate from 35/min to 42/min
q.e: A plateau pressure above 30 cm H2O in ARDS calls for decreasing VT in 1-mL/kg steps (minimum 4 mL/kg), here 6 to 5 mL/kg x 65 kg = 325 mL. Permissive hypercapnia is accepted during lung-protective ventilation but does not justify keeping the plateau pressure above 30 cm H2O. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 21236–21246)
q.src: Permissive hypercapnia in ARDS

q.q: A neonate with severe respiratory distress syndrome is receiving high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) via a CareFusion 3100A with Pmean 16 cm H2O, power/amplitude (ΔP) 3, frequency 12 Hz, %I-time 33%, and FiO2 0.50. Arterial blood gases show pH 7.23, PaCO2 62 torr, and PaO2 64 torr. If power/amplitude is kept unchanged, which frequency adjustment will lower this infant's PaCO2?
o: Decrease the frequency from 12 Hz to 10 Hz
Increase the frequency from 12 Hz to 15 Hz
Keep the frequency unchanged at 12 Hz
Increase the frequency from 12 Hz to 14 Hz
q.e: During HFOV, frequency changes affect CO2 elimination opposite to conventional ventilation: decreasing the HFOV frequency increases tidal volume displacement and lowers the PaCO2, whereas increasing the frequency raises the PaCO2. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 17411–17420, 17478–17493)
q.src: Adjusting HFOV settings for hypercapnia

q.q: An intubated adult is initiated on VC, A/C ventilation with a tidal volume of 500 mL, rate of 14/min, and PEEP of 8 cm H2O. The peak inspiratory pressure (PIP) is consistently 28 cm H2O. How should the respiratory therapist set the low-pressure, high-pressure, and low-PEEP alarms?
o: Low pressure 18 to 23 cm H2O, high pressure 38 to 43 cm H2O, low PEEP 3 to 5 cm H2O
Low pressure 5 to 8 cm H2O, high pressure 60 to 65 cm H2O, low PEEP 0 cm H2O
Low pressure 26 cm H2O, high pressure 30 cm H2O, low PEEP 8 cm H2O
Low pressure 10 cm H2O, high pressure 25 cm H2O, low PEEP 10 cm H2O
q.e: Recommended adult alarm settings are low-pressure at 5 to 10 cm H2O below PIP (18–23 cm H2O), high-pressure limit at 10 to 15 cm H2O above PIP (38–43 cm H2O), and low PEEP/CPAP at 3 to 5 cm H2O below set PEEP (3–5 cm H2O). (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 17610–17637)
q.src: Setting ventilator alarms

q.q: A patient receiving volume-controlled assist/control ventilation with a constant (square) flow of 45 L/min is tachypneic at 28/min and using accessory muscles. The pressure–time scalar shows marked upward concavity ("scalloping") during the inspiratory phase of assisted breaths. Which of the following adjustments should the respiratory therapist make?
o: Increase the inspiratory flow rate or switch to pressure-control ventilation
Decrease the inspiratory flow rate to lengthen the inspiratory time
Decrease the trigger sensitivity to make the ventilator harder to trigger
Add a 1.0-second inspiratory pause to stabilize the pressure waveform
q.e: Scalloping (concavity) of the inspiratory pressure waveform during volume-controlled assisted breaths indicates inadequate inspiratory flow (flow starvation); it is corrected by increasing flow, changing the flow pattern, or switching to pressure control. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 17895–17925)
q.src: Flow asynchrony on ventilator graphics

q.q: An intubated patient on volume-controlled assist/control ventilation (VT 420 mL, rate 16/min, flow 60 L/min) is agitated, and the ventilator graphics display shows two consecutive machine breaths delivered without an expiratory interval between them on most patient efforts. Which of the following changes will correct this asynchrony?
o: Increase the set tidal volume or increase the inspiratory flow
Decrease the set tidal volume and shorten the inspiratory time
Decrease the trigger sensitivity from −1 to −5 cm H2O
Drain condensate from the circuit tubing and replace the HME
q.e: Two consecutive machine breaths triggered without an interval between them is double triggering, caused by patient inspiratory demand exceeding the set volume or inspiratory time; in volume control, it is corrected by increasing the set VT or inspiratory flow (or switching to PC/PS and lengthening inspiratory time). (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 17845–17878)
q.src: Double triggering on ventilator graphics

q.q: A respiratory therapist is performing a pressure-control lung recruitment maneuver at PEEP 20 cm H2O and PIP 40 cm H2O on a sedated patient with ARDS. Ninety seconds into the maneuver, the patient's mean arterial pressure falls from 74 mm Hg to 56 mm Hg, heart rate rises from 98/min to 146/min, and SpO2 drops from 92% to 86%. Which of the following should the therapist do?
o: Terminate the recruitment maneuver immediately and return to prior settings
Increase PEEP to 25 cm H2O and PIP to 45 cm H2O for the remaining 90 seconds
Maintain the current pressures for 3 minutes to complete alveolar recruitment
Switch immediately to a sustained CPAP inflation of 40 cm H2O for 40 seconds
q.e: A lung recruitment maneuver must be terminated immediately if mean arterial pressure falls below 60 to 65 mm Hg, SpO2 drops by more than 4%, heart rate rises above 140/min or falls below 60/min, or new air leaks or arrhythmias develop. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 17960–17980)
q.src: Lung recruitment maneuver termination

q.q: Following a recruitment maneuver at 24 cm H2O PEEP, a respiratory therapist performs a decremental PEEP study in volume control by lowering PEEP in 2-cm H2O steps every 4 minutes. Static compliance (CRS) is 31 mL/cm H2O at PEEP 20, 35 mL/cm H2O at PEEP 18, 39 mL/cm H2O at PEEP 16, and 33 mL/cm H2O at PEEP 14. After repeating the recruitment maneuver, at what PEEP level should the ventilator be set?
o: 18 cm H2O
16 cm H2O
14 cm H2O
20 cm H2O
q.e: In a decremental PEEP study, after identifying the PEEP level that yields the highest static compliance (39 mL/cm H2O at 16 cm H2O) and repeating the recruitment procedure, optimal PEEP is set 2 cm H2O above the level that produced the highest compliance (16 + 2 = 18 cm H2O). (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 18023–18054)
q.src: Decremental PEEP study after recruitment maneuver

sections.title: III-D · Administer Medications and Specialty Gases

q.q: During a cardiopulmonary resuscitation emergency in which intravenous access cannot be established, which of the following medications can be administered directly via endotracheal instillation, and how should the dose be adjusted relative to the intravenous dose?
o: Lidocaine, epinephrine, atropine, or naloxone at 2 to 2.5 times the IV dose, diluted in 10 mL
Amiodarone, adenosine, dopamine, or sodium bicarbonate at 1.5 times the IV dose, undiluted
Lidocaine, epinephrine, calcium chloride, or magnesium at 0.5 times the IV dose, in 5 mL
Epinephrine, norepinephrine, furosemide, or midazolam at 4 to 5 times the IV dose, in 20 mL
q.e: When IV access is unavailable in an emergency, lidocaine, epinephrine, atropine, or naloxone (L-E-A-N) can be instilled down the endotracheal tube at a dose 2 to 2.5 times greater than the IV dose, diluted with 10 mL of sterile water or saline. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 18733–18748)
q.src: Endotracheal drug instillation

q.q: When initiating inhaled nitric oxide (INO) therapy for a term neonate with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN), what is the recommended initial INO dose and the maximum acceptable nitrogen dioxide (NO2) level?
o: Initial INO dose of 20 ppm, with NO2 levels not exceeding 2 to 3 ppm
Initial INO dose of 80 ppm, with NO2 levels not exceeding 10 to 12 ppm
Initial INO dose of 2 ppm, with NO2 levels not exceeding 0.5 ppm
Initial INO dose of 40 ppm, with NO2 levels not exceeding 5 to 8 ppm
q.e: The recommended starting dose of inhaled nitric oxide is 20 ppm (often reduced to 5–6 ppm), and monitored nitrogen dioxide (NO2) levels must not exceed 2 to 3 ppm. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 18818–18826, 18878–18885)
q.src: Inhaled nitric oxide dosing and toxicity

q.q: An intubated adult receiving volume-controlled ventilation with flow triggering set at 5 L/min and a heat and moisture exchanger (HME) at the wye is ordered to receive an albuterol treatment via a vibrating mesh nebulizer. Which of the following actions should the respiratory therapist take before starting the treatment?
o: Remove the HME from the circuit and reduce the flow trigger setting to 2 L/min
Leave the HME in place to warm the aerosol and increase flow trigger to 6 L/min
Place the vibrating mesh nebulizer in the expiratory limb just before the filter
Decrease the set tidal volume by 150 mL to compensate for added nebulizer flow
q.e: Before administering aerosolized medications to a mechanically ventilated patient, the HME must be removed because it traps aerosol particles, and flow triggering should be set to 2 L/min because high bias flow dilutes the aerosol and increases washout. Vibrating mesh nebulizers add no flow or volume to the circuit. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 18694–18722)
q.src: Inhaled medication delivery during mechanical ventilation

sections.title: III-E · Make or Recommend Changes to the Respiratory Care Plan

q.q: An alert intubated adult completes a 60-minute spontaneous breathing trial with a patent upper airway, a positive gag reflex, an audible cuff leak, a maximum expiratory pressure (MEP) of 72 cm H2O, and a peak cough flow of 75 L/min. Which of the following should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Proceed with extubation because airway protection and cough clearance criteria are met
Postpone extubation until the maximum expiratory pressure exceeds 90 cm H2O
Postpone extubation until the spontaneous peak cough flow exceeds 120 L/min
Perform a tracheotomy because secretion clearance remains inadequate for extubation
q.e: An alert patient who completes an SBT with a patent upper airway, intact gag reflex, adequate cuff leak, and effective cough clearance (MEP > 60 cm H2O and/or peak cough flow > 60 L/min) meets all criteria for extubation. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 19544–19559)
q.src: Extubation readiness criteria

q.q: Thirty minutes after extubation, an adult patient has a PaCO2 of 39 torr, a pH of 7.41, and mild hypoxemia with an SpO2 of 88% while receiving oxygen via a simple mask at 6 L/min. To avoid reintubation, which of the following should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Switch to a high-flow nasal cannula at 20–40 L/min and titrate the FiO2 as needed
Initiate noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation to reduce the arterial PaCO2
Decrease the simple mask input flow to 2 L/min to prevent oxygen-induced apnea
Switch to a standard nasal cannula at 2 L/min with an inline heat-moisture exchanger
q.e: To avoid reintubation in patients who develop mild to moderate hypoxemia after extubation without hypercapnia, a high-flow nasal cannula at 20–40 L/min with FiO2 titration is recommended; NPPV is used when mild to moderate hypercapnia develops after extubation. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 20251–20263, 20738–20740)
q.src: Post-extubation hypoxemia management

q.q: A mechanically ventilated patient receiving inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm for pulmonary arterial hypertension has a rise in blood methemoglobin from 0.8% to 2.4% while oxygenation remains stable. Which of the following modifications should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Decrease the inhaled nitric oxide dosage as tolerated and continue to monitor
Discontinue the inhaled nitric oxide abruptly to stop methemoglobin formation
Increase the inhaled nitric oxide dosage in 5-ppm increments to improve perfusion
Switch the delivery system to a negative-pressure room with an inline HME filter
q.e: When methemoglobin (MetHg) increases above 1.5% during inhaled nitric oxide therapy, the dosage should be decreased as tolerated while continuing to monitor; abrupt discontinuation is avoided because iNO must be weaned in small increments (3–5 ppm) to prevent a rebound effect. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 20403–20419)
q.src: Inhaled nitric oxide modification for methemoglobinemia

q.q: A patient with pulmonary edema secondary to congestive heart failure requires diuretic therapy, and recent laboratory results show a serum potassium level of 3.1 mEq/L. Which of the following medications should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: A potassium-sparing diuretic such as amiloride (Midamor)
A quick-acting loop diuretic such as furosemide (Lasix)
An osmotic mucolytic agent such as 7% hypertonic saline
A nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker such as vecuronium
q.e: Although a loop diuretic such as furosemide is generally recommended for pulmonary edema due to CHF, a potassium-sparing diuretic such as amiloride (Midamor) should be recommended instead when serum potassium is low (< 3.5 mEq/L). (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 20538–20544)
q.src: Diuretic selection in hypokalemia

q.q: A premature newborn delivered at 27 weeks' gestation is intubated in the delivery room and exhibits early signs of infant respiratory distress syndrome. To decrease the risk of pneumothorax and pulmonary interstitial emphysema, which of the following should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Administer prophylactic exogenous surfactant rather than waiting for rescue dosing
Withhold exogenous surfactant until chest x-ray confirms a tension pneumothorax
Restrict therapy to a single rescue dose of surfactant after 48 hours of ventilation
Instill nebulized 10% acetylcysteine through the endotracheal tube before ventilation
q.e: Prophylactic administration of exogenous surfactant rather than rescue administration is recommended—especially in infants of < 30 weeks' gestation—because it decreases the risk of pneumothorax, pulmonary interstitial emphysema, and neonatal mortality. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 20544–20562)
q.src: Exogenous surfactant therapy in premature neonates

q.q: A physician orders 2 mL of 20% acetylcysteine by nebulizer for a patient with retained, tenacious secretions, but only 10% acetylcysteine is available on the unit. Which of the following should the respiratory therapist do?
o: Administer 4 mL (twice the volume) of the diluted 10% acetylcysteine
Administer 1 mL of the 10% acetylcysteine mixed with 3 mL of saline
Administer 2 mL of the 10% acetylcysteine at double the oxygen flow
Substitute 2 mL of 3% hypertonic saline without calling the doctor
q.e: When 2 mL of 20% acetylcysteine is ordered and only 10% acetylcysteine is available, the therapist should administer 4 mL (twice the volume) of the more diluted 10% solution to deliver the ordered drug mass. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 20596–20602)
q.src: Acetylcysteine concentration and volume adjustment

q.q: During a small-volume nebulizer treatment with albuterol, an adult patient's heart rate increases from a baseline of 88/min to 116/min. Which of the following actions should the respiratory therapist take?
o: Stop the treatment, monitor the patient, notify the nurse and doctor, and recommend a dose reduction or levalbuterol
Continue the nebulizer treatment at half the gas flow rate and recheck the heart rate 30 minutes after completion
Add 3 mL of normal saline to the nebulizer cup and instruct the patient to breathe slowly with an inspiratory pause
Switch the medication immediately to racemic epinephrine 2.25% to stabilize the heart rate while relieving bronchospasm
q.e: If a patient's heart rate increases by more than 20% during a SABA bronchodilator treatment, the therapist should stop the treatment, monitor the patient, notify the nurse and physician, and recommend a dose reduction or a drug with minimal beta-1 side effects such as levalbuterol. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 20570–20585, 20761–20764)
q.src: Adverse tachycardia during SABA therapy

q.q: An agitated mechanically ventilated patient with patient-ventilator asynchrony develops hypotension (blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg) and cardiac depression during a midazolam infusion. Which of the following sedatives should the respiratory therapist recommend as an alternative?
o: Dexmedetomidine hydrochloride (Precedex)
Intravenous propofol (Diprivan) infusion
Intravenous morphine sulfate bolus dosing
Succinylcholine (Anectine) continuous drip
q.e: Cardiac depression and hypotension are seen mainly with midazolam or propofol; in this situation, dexmedetomidine hydrochloride (Precedex) is recommended for sedation because it has less effect on blood pressure and respiratory drive. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 20484–20503)
q.src: Sedative selection with hemodynamic instability

q.q: A mechanically ventilated adult with dense right-sided lobar consolidation and a clear left lung on chest radiograph has a PaO2 of 54 torr on an FiO2 of 0.50. Which of the following position changes should the respiratory therapist recommend to improve oxygenation?
o: Place the patient in the left lateral decubitus (good-lung-down) position
Place the patient in the right lateral decubitus (bad-lung) position
Place the patient in the Trendelenburg (15-degree head-down) position
Keep the patient flat in the supine position without lateral rotation
q.e: For a mechanically ventilated patient with unilateral lung disease such as lobar consolidation or atelectasis, placing the patient in the 'good-lung-down' position (left lung down when the right lung is consolidated) improves ventilation-perfusion matching and oxygenation. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 19656–19663, 20667–20671)
q.src: Patient positioning in unilateral lung disease

q.q: Following extubation after 12 days of invasive mechanical ventilation, a patient is unable to swallow liquids without coughing and has difficulty speaking clearly. Consultation with which of the following specialists should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Speech-language therapist
Pulmonary allergist doctor
Occupational therapy team
Child life support worker
q.e: When a patient is unable to swallow and speak properly after extubation or decannulation following prolonged mechanical ventilation or artificial airway use, a consultation with a speech-language therapist should be recommended. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 19580–19607)
q.src: Recommending specialist consultation after extubation

sections.title: III-F · Use Evidence-Based Practice

q.q: According to National Asthma Education and Prevention Program (NAEPP) guidelines, at what interval should follow-up visits be scheduled when a step-down in asthma therapy is anticipated?
o: Every 3 months
Every 1–2 weeks
Every 1–2 years
Every 6–9 months
q.e: Under NAEPP EPR-3 guidelines, patients should be seen every 2–6 weeks while gaining control, every 1–6 months to monitor control, and every 3 months if a step-down in therapy is anticipated. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 21020–21035)
q.src: NAEPP follow-up interval for asthma step-down

q.q: A patient with ARDS is ventilated under the ARDSNet protocol with a tidal volume of 6 mL/kg PBW and a set respiratory rate of 35/min. Arterial blood gas analysis reveals a pH of 7.11 and a plateau pressure of 29 cm H2O. Which of the following changes should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Increase VT in 1-mL/kg steps until the pH exceeds 7.15 and consider NaHCO3
Increase the ventilator respiratory rate to 40/min and keep VT at 6 mL/kg
Decrease VT in 1-mL/kg steps to 4 mL/kg to keep Pplat below 25 cm H2O
Maintain current settings because permissive hypercapnia allows a pH of 7.10
q.e: Under the ARDSNet protocol, the maximum ventilator rate is 35/min; if the rate is already 35/min and the pH remains below 7.15, VT should be increased in 1-mL/kg steps until the pH is greater than 7.15 (even if the Pplat target is exceeded) and NaHCO3 administration considered. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 21240–21259)
q.src: ARDSNet management of severe acidosis at maximum rate

q.q: A patient in GOLD COPD Category D (FEV1 42% of predicted and 2 exacerbations requiring hospitalization in the past year) continues to experience persistent dyspnea despite adherent therapy with a combined LAMA and LABA. According to GOLD guidelines, which of the following should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Step up to triple combination therapy with a LAMA, a LABA, and an inhaled steroid
Discontinue the LAMA and switch to monotherapy with an inhaled corticosteroid
Step down to an as-needed short-acting bronchodilator without controller therapy
Replace the inhaled bronchodilators with daily oral prednisone monotherapy
q.e: For patients in GOLD Category D (<= 49% predicted spirometry, >= 2 exacerbations per year with at least one hospitalization), first-line therapy is a LAMA plus a LABA; if symptoms persist, triple combination therapy with a LAMA, a LABA, and inhaled steroids is recommended. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 21411–21422)
q.src: GOLD Category D COPD pharmacologic therapy

sections.title: III-G · Provide Respiratory Care in High-Risk Situations

q.q: Which of the following adult findings is a standard criterion for activating the medical emergency team (MET) to intervene before cardiopulmonary arrest?
o: Respiratory rate < 8/min or > 30/min, or heart rate < 40/min or > 130/min
Respiratory rate < 12/min or > 20/min, or heart rate < 60/min or > 100/min
Systolic blood pressure < 110 mm Hg or urine output < 100 mL over 4 hours
Pulse oximetry SpO2 < 95% on room air with a normal level of consciousness
q.e: Adult MET/RRT activation criteria include an acute change in mental status, heart rate < 40 or > 130/min, respiratory rate < 8/min or > 30/min, systolic BP < 90 mm Hg, SpO2 < 90% (especially with supplemental O2), or urine output < 50 mL over 4 hours. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 22228–22238)
q.src: Medical emergency team activation criteria

q.q: When preparing to transport an intubated pediatric patient, below what patient weight threshold must the portable ventilator be specifically certified for pediatric use to accurately deliver small tidal volumes and high rates?
o: 15 kg (33 lb)
10 kg (22 lb)
25 kg (55 lb)
30 kg (66 lb)
q.e: For intubated children weighing less than 15 kg (33 lb), the transport ventilator must be certified for pediatric use and able to accurately deliver the smaller tidal volumes and higher respiratory rates required. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 22356–22363)
q.src: Pediatric transport ventilator weight criterion

q.q: A mechanically ventilated patient requiring an FiO2 of 0.85 and 5 cm H2O of PEEP at sea level is being prepared for air transport in an aircraft with a cabin altitude of 8000 feet (Pb 565 torr). Because an FiO2 equivalent to 0.80 or higher at sea level cannot be delivered at 8000 feet, what should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Increase the PEEP level on the transport ventilator to ensure adequate oxygenation
Decrease the FiO2 to 0.50 during the climb to prevent nitrogen-washout atelectasis
Inflate the endotracheal tube cuff with sterile water and remove all PEEP support
Rely on noncalibrated end-tidal CO2 readings to titrate the inspired oxygen fraction
q.e: At an altitude of 8000 feet or higher, a clinician cannot provide an FiO2 equivalent to 0.80 or more at sea level; therefore, patients requiring 80% or more O2 at sea level must be placed on PEEP/CPAP or have their PEEP levels raised to maintain adequate oxygenation. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 22503–22522)
q.src: Air transport oxygenation for high-FiO2 patients

q.q: A patient who underwent a surgical tracheotomy 18 hours ago accidentally decannulates during turning, and the SpO2 drops to 81%. After calling for help, which of the following should the respiratory therapist do?
o: Occlude the stoma with a sterile petroleum jelly gauze pad and provide bag-mask ventilation with O2
