Forcefully reinsert the same tracheostomy tube blindly into the fresh stoma tract without a stylet
Apply a 40% tracheostomy collar over the open neck stoma and wait for the surgeon to arrive
Insert a supraglottic airway through the neck stoma and ventilate with a flow-inflating bag
q.e: When accidental decannulation occurs in a patient with a fresh tracheostomy, the clinician should call for help, occlude the stoma with a sterile petroleum jelly gauze pad, and provide bag-mask ventilation with oxygen via the upper airway; blind reinsertion into a fresh tract is avoided. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 21844–21854)
q.src: Accidental decannulation of a fresh tracheostomy

q.q: A 2-month-old infant on pressure-control ventilation develops sudden hypotension, a sharp drop in delivered tidal volume, absent left breath sounds, and a left tension pneumothorax. Which angiocath size and insertion site should be used for emergency needle thoracostomy?
o: An 18- or 20-gauge angiocath in the second intercostal space over the top of the third rib in the midclavicular line
A 14-gauge angiocath in the fourth intercostal space along the inferior border of the fourth rib in the midaxillary line
An 18- or 20-gauge angiocath in the fifth intercostal space below the fifth rib along the posterior axillary line
A 14-gauge angiocath in the second intercostal space below the second rib along the anterior sternal border
q.e: Emergency needle thoracostomy for a tension pneumothorax uses a 14-gauge angiocath for adults or an 18- or 20-gauge angiocath for infants, inserted into the second intercostal space over the top of the third rib in the midclavicular line. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 21972–21993)
q.src: Needle thoracostomy in an infant tension pneumothorax

sections.title: III-H · Assist a Physician or Provider in Performing Procedures

q.q: When assisting a physician with specialized bronchoscopy to evaluate a peripheral lung lesion, how does electromagnetic navigational bronchoscopy (ENB) guide the bronchoscope to the target?
o: Low-frequency electromagnetic waves from a board below the chest create a real-time 3D image
An ultrasonic transducer at the scope tip images central lymph nodes through the airway wall
A 120-degree hockey-stick lighted stylet transilluminates the anterior neck below the thyroid
Continuous fluoroscopic x-ray beams track a radiopaque balloon catheter into the pleural space
q.e: ENB uses low-frequency electromagnetic waves transmitted from a magnetic board placed below the patient's chest to visualize peripheral lung lesions in three dimensions (3D) and in real time, whereas EBUS combines bronchoscopy with ultrasound. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 23204–23225)
q.src: Electromagnetic navigational bronchoscopy mechanism

q.q: The respiratory therapist is assisting with synchronized cardioversion of an adult patient in atrial flutter whose ventricular rate remains 162/min despite antiarrhythmic medication. With the biphasic cardioverter set to Sync mode, which initial energy level should be selected?
q.e: For synchronized biphasic cardioversion in adults, the recommended initial energy level is 50–100 J for atrial flutter, 120–200 J for atrial fibrillation, and 100 J for stable monomorphic VT with a pulse. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 23444–23454, 23939–23942)
q.src: Synchronized cardioversion energy level for atrial flutter

q.q: During a bedside bronchoscopy under moderate sedation, the respiratory therapist evaluates the patient using the Richmond Agitation Sedation Scale (RASS). The patient opens his eyes and moves in response to voice without making eye contact, with an SpO2 of 95% and respiratory rate of 14/min. How should the therapist interpret this finding?
o: The patient is at the targeted RASS score of -3 for moderate sedation
The patient is oversedated at a RASS score of -4 and needs naloxone
The patient is lightly sedated at a RASS score of -2 and needs bolus
The patient is unarousable at a RASS score of -5 and needs a tube
q.e: On the Richmond Agitation Sedation Scale (RASS), movement or eye opening to voice without eye contact corresponds to a score of -3 (moderate sedation), which is the targeted score for moderately sedated patients. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 23486–23521)
q.src: Richmond Agitation Sedation Scale assessment during moderate sedation

q.q: A conscious, ventilator-dependent adult and the family consent to withdrawal of ventilatory support via terminal weaning. After morphine and midazolam are titrated for comfort and the FiO2 is lowered to 30%, which of the following ventilator adjustments should the respiratory therapist make to perform terminal weaning?
o: Set IMV at 12/min, remove PEEP and pressure support, disable alarms, and step the rate to zero over 30–60 minutes
Disconnect the ventilator immediately, deflate the cuff, remove the endotracheal tube, and apply a 2-L/min cannula
Disconnect the ventilator immediately and place the endotracheal tube on a 28–35% humidified T-tube adapter
Maintain assist-control ventilation with 10 cm H2O PEEP while increasing sedation above comfort levels to hasten death
q.e: For terminal weaning (used in conscious or altered-consciousness patients with the airway left in place), the ventilator is set to IMV at a normal rate (12/min for adults), PEEP and pressure support are removed, apnea/backup ventilation and alarms are disabled, and the IMV rate is progressively stepped down to zero over 30 to 60 minutes. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 23731–23749, 23803–23838)
q.src: Terminal weaning procedure during withdrawal of life support

sections.title: III-I · Interact with Team Members, Patients, and Families

q.q: When reviewing objective memory data downloaded from a home CPAP unit for a patient with obstructive sleep apnea, which minimum usage threshold defines good CPAP adherence?
o: At least 4 hours per night for at least 5 nights per week
At least 2 hours per night for at least 3 nights per week
At least 6 hours per night for at least 7 nights per week
At least 8 hours per night for at least 6 nights per week
q.e: Good CPAP adherence is defined as use of the device for a minimum of four hours per night at least five nights per week. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 25404–25414)
q.src: Definition of good CPAP adherence

q.q: A hospitalized patient with COPD is being evaluated 24 hours before discharge for home oxygen reimbursement. On room air at rest, the arterial PaO2 is 58 mm Hg and the SaO2 is 89%. Which of the following additional findings qualifies this patient for home oxygen coverage?
o: Erythrocythemia with a hematocrit of 58% or cor pulmonale
A smoking history of 40 pack-years with a daily cough
An FEV1 of 65% of predicted on bedside spirometry testing
A resting respiratory rate of 22/min with pursed-lip breathing
q.e: While resting room-air PaO2 <= 55 torr or SpO2 <= 88% qualifies directly, patients with a PaO2 of 56–59 mm Hg or oxygen saturation of 89% qualify if they also have dependent edema suggesting CHF, pulmonary hypertension or cor pulmonale, or erythrocythemia with a hematocrit higher than 56%. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 24258–24285)
q.src: Medicare home oxygen qualification with PaO2 56–59 mm Hg

q.q: A 60-year-old patient with COPD is performing aerobic cycling in a pulmonary rehabilitation program. Using the predicted maximum heart rate formula (220 - age), what target heart rate range (60% to 75% of predicted maximum) should the respiratory therapist use to achieve optimal cardiovascular benefit?
o: 96 to 120/min
80 to 96/min
120 to 136/min
136 to 160/min
q.e: For a 60-year-old patient, the predicted maximum heart rate (220 - age) is 160/min; the targeted exercise heart rate of 60% to 75% of predicted maximum is 96/min (0.60 x 160) to 120/min (0.75 x 160). (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 24779–24789)
q.src: Pulmonary rehabilitation target exercise heart rate calculation

q.q: An interdisciplinary team is preparing a stable tracheostomized patient on volume-controlled ventilation (FiO2 0.30, PEEP 5 cm H2O) for home discharge. The patient can tolerate only 2 hours of spontaneous breathing off the ventilator and lives in a rural area 3 hours from the equipment provider. Which of the following must be included in the discharge plan?
o: Provide a backup ventilator in the home and notify the local utility company in writing
Cancel home discharge because any PEEP requirement contraindicates home ventilation
Provide a single ventilator with a 60-minute internal battery and a nasal pillow mask
Switch the patient to a chest cuirass negative-pressure ventilator without a backup
q.e: A backup ventilator must be provided in the home for patients who cannot maintain spontaneous ventilation for 4 or more hours or who live where a replacement ventilator cannot be provided within 2 hours; for rural patients with power outage risks, the utility company should also be notified in writing. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 25198–25226, 25249–25253)
q.src: Home mechanical ventilation backup ventilator requirements

q.q: During a non-emergent inpatient asthma assessment and education session, the respiratory therapist finds that the patient has limited English proficiency, while an adult family member offers to translate and notes that the patient practices yoga breathing exercises for asthma. Which of the following actions should the respiratory therapist take?
o: Request a certified medical translator and recommend including the yoga exercises in the care plan if not contraindicated
Use the adult family member to translate the medical interview and instruct the patient to stop the yoga breathing routine
Postpone the asthma education until after discharge and leave standard English-language instruction sheets at the bedside
Have the patient sign the asthma action plan without an interpreter and document the prescribed pharmacologic regimen
q.e: When a language barrier exists in a non-emergency setting, the therapist should request a certified medical translator rather than using family members (due to privacy and accuracy concerns), and non-contraindicated alternative health practices such as yoga for asthma should be recommended for inclusion in the care plan. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 3055–3063, 3148–3165)
q.src: Culturally aware and linguistically appropriate patient interaction

sections.title: Clinical judgment · Adult chronic lung disease: intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation

q.q: A 34-year-old adult is intubated and receiving volume-control assist/control mechanical ventilation (VT 450 mL, rate 12/min, PEEP 5 cm H2O, FiO2 0.40) in the ICU for status asthmaticus. Over the past hour, the peak inspiratory pressure (PIP) has risen from 32 to 48 cm H2O while breath sounds remain bilateral and wheezy. Which of the following bedside maneuvers should the respiratory therapist perform first to differentiate increased airway resistance from decreased respiratory system compliance?
o: Apply an end-inspiratory pause of 0.5 to 2.0 seconds to measure the plateau pressure
Apply an end-expiratory pause of 0.5 to 2.0 seconds to measure the total PEEP level
Order an immediate portable anteroposterior chest film to check endotracheal tube depth
Perform a sustained lung recruitment maneuver at 40 cm H2O of CPAP for 40 seconds
q.e: During volume-control ventilation, an end-inspiratory pause (0.5–2.0 sec) measures plateau pressure (Pplat) and partitions driving pressure into airway resistance (PIP − Pplat) and respiratory system compliance (Pplat − PEEP). An end-expiratory pause measures auto-PEEP rather than Pplat. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 5219–5234, 5270–5290)
q.src: Partitioning peak airway pressure during volume-control ventilation

q.q: A 28-year-old adult (predicted body weight 65 kg) with life-threatening status asthmaticus is intubated in the ICU on volume-control ventilation at a VT of 450 mL, rate of 12/min, FiO2 of 0.50, PEEP of 0 cm H2O, and I:E ratio of 1:2. An arterial blood gas shows pH 7.24, PaCO2 64 torr, and PaO2 88 torr, and an inspiratory hold shows a plateau pressure of 29 cm H2O with air trapping. Which of the following ventilator management strategies should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Increase inspiratory flow to achieve an I:E ratio of 1:4 or 1:5 and accept high PaCO2 since pH > 7.2
Increase the mandatory respiratory rate to 22/min to rapidly lower the PaCO2 into the normal range
Increase the set tidal volume to 650 mL to boost alveolar minute ventilation and normalize the pH
Decrease the inspiratory flow rate to lengthen inspiratory time and add 12 cm H2O of external PEEP
q.e: In mechanically ventilated asthma patients, use high flows during volume-control ventilation to shorten inspiratory time and provide an I:E ratio of 1:4 or 1:5 while keeping plateau pressure ≤ 30 cm H2O and accepting a high PaCO2 as long as pH > 7.2 (permissive hypercapnia). Raising rate or VT worsens air trapping and hyperinflation. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 30611–30637)
q.src: Mechanical ventilation and permissive hypercapnia in status asthmaticus

q.q: A 69-year-old adult with severe emphysema is intubated and receiving volume-control assist/control ventilation (VT 480 mL, rate 10/min, inspiratory flow 70 L/min, I:E ratio 1:5, PEEP 0 cm H2O). Ventilator scalars show frequent patient inspiratory efforts that fail to trigger a breath, and an end-expiratory pause reveals an auto-PEEP of 10 cm H2O from small airway collapse. Which of the following ventilator adjustments should the respiratory therapist recommend to reduce the work of triggering?
o: Apply external PEEP incrementally at 5 to 8 cm H2O (50–80% of the measured auto-PEEP)
Apply external PEEP at 12 to 15 cm H2O so that circuit pressure exceeds the auto-PEEP
Decrease the inspiratory flow rate to 40 L/min to prolong the mechanical inspiratory time
Make the ventilator trigger sensitivity less sensitive to eliminate wasted patient efforts
q.e: When auto-PEEP is caused by small airway collapse or decreased elastic recoil in COPD and impairs triggering, incremental external PEEP up to 50–80% of the measured auto-PEEP (5–8 cm H2O for 10 cm H2O of auto-PEEP) counteracts the threshold load. Setting external PEEP above auto-PEEP worsens hyperinflation. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 7514–7519, 17825–17835)
q.src: External PEEP for auto-PEEP and ineffective triggering in COPD

q.q: A 67-year-old adult intubated for an acute exacerbation of COPD (baseline pH 7.38, PaCO2 52 torr, respiratory rate 16/min, heart rate 88/min on volume-control ventilation) begins a spontaneous breathing trial (SBT) on CPAP 5 cm H2O and FiO2 0.35. Twenty minutes into the trial, the patient develops diaphoresis, thoracoabdominal paradox, a respiratory rate of 36/min, a heart rate of 126/min, pH 7.26, and PaCO2 68 torr. Which of the following actions should the respiratory therapist take next?
o: Return the patient to ventilatory support, work to correct the causes, and repeat an SBT in 24 hours
Continue the spontaneous breathing trial for a full 30 minutes before making any ventilator changes
Extubate the patient immediately and initiate noninvasive bilevel positive airway pressure by mask
Increase the CPAP level to 10 cm H2O and repeat the arterial blood gas at the 60-minute mark
q.e: This patient exhibits objective and subjective SBT failure (pH < 7.30, PaCO2 rise > 10 torr, RR > 30–35/min, HR > 120/min, diaphoresis, and thoracoabdominal paradox). When a patient fails an SBT, return the patient to ventilatory support to prevent muscle fatigue, determine and correct the causes, and resume performing an SBT every 24 hours. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 7524–7560)
q.src: Managing spontaneous breathing trial failure in COPD

q.q: A 70-year-old adult man (predicted body weight 82 kg) with an acute exacerbation of COPD is intubated in the emergency department with a size 6.5-mm oral endotracheal tube and placed on volume-control ventilation. During the initial ventilator check, loud inspiratory gurgling is heard over the trachea, exhaled tidal volume is 140 mL below the set volume, and a cuff pressure of 38 cm H2O is required to stop the leak. Which of the following actions should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Keep cuff pressure below 25–30 cm H2O and recommend exchanging the tube for a larger size
Maintain the cuff inflation pressure at 38 cm H2O to preserve a leak-free seal on inspiration
Withdraw the endotracheal tube by 4 cm and recheck cuff pressure with a calibrated manometer
Switch the ventilator to pressure-control mode and deflate the cuff for minimal leak technique
q.e: After intubation, if cuff pressures > 30 cm H2O are required to prevent air leakage, the endotracheal tube is likely too small for the patient's airway. Cuff pressure should be kept below 25–30 cm H2O to avoid mucosal ischemia, and the tube should be exchanged for a larger size (or one with continuous subglottic suction). (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 5646–5654, 7674–7688)
q.src: Managing endotracheal cuff leak from an undersized tube

sections.title: Clinical judgment · Adult chronic lung disease: noninvasive management

q.q: A 72-year-old adult with severe COPD who takes daily oral maintenance theophylline presents to the emergency department with worsening dyspnea, palpitations, and nausea. The patient is afebrile (36.9°C) with scant clear sputum, an SpO2 of 90% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula, and occasional premature ventricular contractions on the ECG monitor. Which of the following diagnostic tests should the respiratory therapist recommend obtaining next?
o: Serum theophylline concentration level
Bedside forced expiratory spirometry
Expectorated sputum culture and Gram stain
Routine transthoracic echocardiography
q.e: In a patient with COPD taking theophylline who presents with an acute exacerbation and premature ventricular contractions, a serum theophylline level should be obtained because theophylline can cause PVCs. In acute COPD exacerbations, spirometry is of little value, sputum culture is indicated when infection is suspected (fever, purulent sputum), and echocardiography is not routinely ordered. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 2406–2412, 26821–26836)
q.src: Diagnostic evaluation during an acute COPD exacerbation

q.q: A 22-year-old adult with known cystic fibrosis presents to the emergency department with 3 days of fever, increased purulent sputum, fatigue, poor appetite, and labored breathing with intercostal retractions. Pulse oximetry shows an SpO2 of 87% on room air, and a complete blood count demonstrates leukocytosis. In addition to a chest radiograph, which of the following laboratory studies should the respiratory therapist recommend obtaining to evaluate this patient's acute status?
o: Serum sodium, chloride, and potassium levels with an arterial blood gas
Repeat quantitative sweat chloride testing with CFTR mutation analysis
Serum alpha1-antitrypsin titer with total immunoglobulin E concentration
Single-breath carbon monoxide diffusing capacity with plethysmography
q.e: In a patient with cystic fibrosis seen in the ED for acute respiratory distress, diagnostic testing should evaluate for low serum Na+, Cl−, and K+, hypochloremic metabolic acidosis, and moderate hypoxemia (SpO2 < 90% on room air) via electrolytes and ABG analysis. Sweat chloride testing is used for initial diagnosis rather than acute exacerbation assessment. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 28730–28747)
q.src: Laboratory evaluation in an acute cystic fibrosis exacerbation

q.q: A 68-year-old alert, cooperative adult with an acute exacerbation of COPD and respiratory acidosis (pH 7.28, PaCO2 64 torr, PaO2 61 torr) is ordered to start noninvasive bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) at 10/5 cm H2O via an oronasal mask in the emergency department. As the respiratory therapist approaches with the mask, the patient becomes anxious about having it strapped tightly over his face. Which of the following actions should the respiratory therapist take to initiate the therapy?
o: Position the patient in high semi-Fowler’s and hold the mask in place without strapping until he adjusts
Place the patient supine, strap the mask tightly at once, and request an intravenous propofol bolus
Insert a heat and moisture exchanger between the mask and the circuit to warm the inspired gas
Increase the initial IPAP setting to 26 cm H2O so the higher flow relieves his sensation of dyspnea
q.e: When initiating BiPAP for acute respiratory failure, position the patient in a high semi-Fowler’s (sitting) position and hold the interface in place without strapping until the patient becomes accustomed to it. IPAP should be kept below 20–25 cm H2O to avoid gastric insufflation, and HMEs are contraindicated during NPPV. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 17275–17296)
q.src: Initiating and coaching noninvasive bilevel ventilation in COPD

q.q: A 54-year-old adult with non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis is admitted to the hospital with an acute exacerbation characterized by dyspnea, diffuse crackles and wheezes, and difficulty expectorating copious, tenacious mucopurulent sputum and mucous plugs. Systemic antibiotic therapy and supplemental oxygen have been started. Which of the following respiratory care regimens should the respiratory therapist recommend to improve bronchial hygiene and reduce airflow obstruction?
o: Aerosol bronchodilator and nebulized hypertonic saline or mucolytic therapy with airway clearance
Continuous positive airway pressure at 15 cm H2O with routine prophylactic antitussive medication
Aerosolized corticosteroid monotherapy with strict fluid restriction and bed rest in the supine position
Dry-powder long-acting beta-agonist monotherapy without airway clearance or hydrating aerosols
q.e: Antibiotics and bronchopulmonary hygiene are the mainstays of bronchiectasis management. During acute exacerbations, recommend aerosol bronchodilators if indicated, nebulized hypertonic saline, mannitol, or mucolytic agents for airway hydration and secretion clearance, and airway clearance therapy to help expectorate tenacious secretions and mucous plugs. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 28871–28898)
q.src: Inpatient management of an acute bronchiectasis exacerbation

q.q: A 31-year-old adult presents to the emergency department with an acute asthma exacerbation and receives supplemental oxygen, three nebulized albuterol and ipratropium treatments over the first hour, and oral systemic corticosteroids. Reassessment 1 hour after treatment shows persistent mild-to-moderate wheezing and dyspnea, an alert sensorium, an SpO2 of 93% on room air, a PaCO2 of 36 torr, and a peak expiratory flow (PEF) of 55% of personal best. Which of the following disposition recommendations should the respiratory therapist make?
o: Admit the patient to a hospital medical unit for continued treatment and monitoring
Discharge the patient home on a short-acting beta-agonist and an inhaled steroid
Admit the patient to the intensive care unit for immediate endotracheal intubation
Keep the patient in the waiting area without further therapy and recheck PEF in 6 hours
q.e: Hospital admission to a medical unit is recommended when mild-to-moderate asthma symptoms continue despite appropriate ED treatment and the FEV1 or PEF is not adequately restored (40–69% of predicted or personal best). Discharge home requires symptom relief and an FEV1 or PEF ≥ 70% sustained for at least 1 hour, whereas ICU admission is indicated if FEV1/PEF remains < 40%, the patient is drowsy/confused, or hypercapnia develops. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 30535–30547, 30605–30610)
q.src: Emergency department disposition for acute asthma exacerbation

q.q: A 65-year-old hospitalized adult with COPD and acute hypoxemic-hypercapnic respiratory failure is receiving bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) at an IPAP of 16 cm H2O, an EPAP of 8 cm H2O, a backup rate of 10/min, and an FiO2 of 0.65. Six hours later, the patient is comfortable with a respiratory rate of 18/min, and an arterial blood gas shows pH 7.38, PaCO2 50 torr, PaO2 114 torr, and SaO2 98%. Which of the following adjustments should the respiratory therapist recommend first?
o: Decrease the FiO2 until it is 0.50 or less while keeping IPAP at 16 and EPAP at 8 cm H2O
Decrease the EPAP from 8 to 4 cm H2O while keeping IPAP at 16 cm H2O and FiO2 at 0.65
Decrease the IPAP from 16 to 10 cm H2O while keeping EPAP at 8 cm H2O and FiO2 at 0.65
Discontinue bilevel positive airway pressure immediately and place the patient on room air
q.e: During BiPAP therapy, when oxygenation improves on a high FiO2, first decrease the FiO2 until it is ≤ 0.50 and then lower the EPAP (keeping ΔP constant to avoid altering the PaCO2). Lowering IPAP alone reduces ΔP and minute ventilation, whereas lowering EPAP alone increases ΔP and leaves the patient exposed to an FiO2 above 0.50. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 17315–17334)
q.src: De-escalating FiO2 and EPAP during bilevel positive airway pressure

sections.title: Clinical judgment · Adult chronic lung disease: outpatient management

q.q: A 24-year-old adult with confirmed cystic fibrosis returns to the outpatient pulmonary clinic for a scheduled 3-month follow-up visit. The patient is clinically stable on a high-energy diet, pancreatic enzymes, daily airway clearance, and inhaled medications, and had a posterior-anterior and lateral chest radiograph 6 months ago. Which of the following assessments and diagnostic studies should the respiratory therapist obtain at this routine clinic visit?
o: Body mass index and nutritional status, FEV1 and SpO2, and a sputum sample for Gram stain and culture
Posterior-anterior and lateral chest radiographs, a repeat sweat chloride test, and an arterial blood gas
High-resolution chest computed tomography, bronchoalveolar lavage, and a 12-lead electrocardiogram
Laboratory polysomnography, single-breath diffusing capacity (DLCO), and a methacholine challenge
q.e: Routine outpatient clinic visits every 2–3 months for stabilized cystic fibrosis patients include assessment of nutritional status and BMI, lung function (FEV1 and SpO2), collection of a sputum sample for Gram stain and culture and sensitivity, assessment of therapy effectiveness, and psychosocial counseling. PA and lateral chest x-rays are obtained every 2–4 years rather than at every clinic visit. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 28794–28802)
q.src: Routine outpatient clinic monitoring in cystic fibrosis

q.q: During a home-care visit, a 25-year-old adult with cystic fibrosis asks the respiratory therapist to review how he cleans his reusable breath-enhanced jet nebulizer. He states that after each treatment he washes the nebulizer parts in dish detergent soap and water, soaks them in household vinegar (acetic acid) for 30 minutes, and rinses them under tap water before air-drying. Which of the following changes to his home nebulizer disinfection routine should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Disinfect by boiling for 5 minutes or soaking in 70% isopropyl alcohol for 5 minutes, and rinse with sterile water
Disinfect by soaking in a 1:50 household bleach dilution for 5 minutes, and rinse thoroughly with warm tap water
Disinfect by soaking in benzalkonium chloride for 10 minutes, and dry the nebulizer parts with a clean paper towel
Continue soaking in household acetic acid for 30 minutes, but rinse with distilled water and store in a plastic bag
q.e: For patients with cystic fibrosis, reusable drug nebulizers should be cleaned with dish soap and water, disinfected by heat (e.g., boiling for 5 minutes, microwaving in water for 5 minutes, dishwasher ≥ 70°C for 30 minutes, or electric steam sterilizer) or cold methods (70% isopropyl alcohol for 5 minutes or 3% hydrogen peroxide for 30 minutes), rinsed with sterile or filtered (≤ 0.2-micron) water, and air-dried. Acetic acid, bleach, and benzalkonium chloride must not be used. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 28812–28829)
q.src: Home cleaning and disinfection of reusable nebulizers in cystic fibrosis

q.q: A 69-year-old outpatient with severe COPD who is already certified for and using continuous long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) at 2 L/min by nasal cannula undergoes home overnight pulse oximetry because of restless sleep and morning cognitive impairment. The overnight recording shows repeated nocturnal desaturation episodes with the SpO2 falling to 83%. Which of the following modifications to the home oxygen regimen should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Titrate the nocturnal oxygen flow upward in 1-L/min increments until the nighttime SpO2 consistently exceeds 88%
Maintain the oxygen flow at 2 L/min overnight because the patient is already receiving continuous daytime oxygen
Switch the patient from the nasal cannula to a simple oxygen mask set at 3 L/min during nighttime sleep hours
Discontinue daytime oxygen therapy and restrict the 2-L/min nasal cannula to nocturnal sleep periods
q.e: For COPD patients already certified for continuous LTOT who exhibit nocturnal desaturation, the oxygen liter flow can be titrated upward in increments of 1 L/min until the nighttime SpO2 consistently exceeds 88% and desaturation events cease. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 7634–7646)
q.src: Managing nocturnal desaturation in COPD on long-term oxygen therapy

sections.title: Clinical judgment · Adult chronic lung disease: evaluation for a new diagnosis

q.q: A 48-year-old adult is referred to the outpatient pulmonary clinic for evaluation of a daily cough productive of tenacious, mucopurulent sputum lasting 2 years and frequent bouts of bronchitis requiring repeated antibiotic courses. Auscultation reveals basilar crackles and wheezes, and a plain chest radiograph shows linear atelectasis and irregular peripheral opacities. Which of the following imaging studies should the respiratory therapist recommend as the diagnostic standard to confirm the suspected diagnosis?
o: High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest
Radionuclide ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) lung scanning
Lateral decubitus chest radiography with B-mode ultrasound
Positron emission tomography (PET) with fluorodeoxyglucose
q.e: High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) and multidetector computed tomography (MDCT) of the chest are the diagnostic standard for confirming bronchiectasis, demonstrating airway dilatation, lack of airway tapering, bronchial wall thickening, and cysts. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 28838–28869)
q.src: Confirming a new diagnosis of non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis

q.q: A 59-year-old adult presents to the outpatient clinic with 6 months of progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry, nonproductive cough. Valid office screening spirometry reveals an FVC of 58% of predicted, an FEV1 of 60% of predicted, and an FEV1/FVC ratio of 83%. To confirm a restrictive disorder and differentiate interstitial lung disease from a chest wall or neuromuscular problem, which of the following evaluations should the respiratory therapist recommend next?
o: Full pulmonary laboratory evaluation with static lung volumes and diffusing capacity (DLCO)
Repeat office spirometry 15 to 30 minutes after an inhaled short-acting bronchodilator
Bronchial provocation challenge with escalating concentrations of nebulized methacholine
Home overnight pulse oximetry to determine the hourly oxygen desaturation index (ODI)
q.e: When screening spirometry suggests a restrictive impairment (reduced FVC with an FEV1/FVC ≥ 70%), the patient should undergo a full evaluation in the pulmonary laboratory including static lung volumes (to confirm a low TLC) and diffusing capacity (DLCO), which is low in interstitial lung diseases such as pulmonary fibrosis and normal in chest wall or neuromuscular disorders. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 7832–7836, 7869–7875)
q.src: Evaluating suspected restrictive lung disease in the pulmonary lab

q.q: A 27-year-old adult being evaluated in the outpatient clinic for a new diagnosis of chronic cough and wheezing occurring 4 days per week (with nighttime awakenings twice per month) undergoes pre- and post-bronchodilator spirometry. Baseline spirometry shows an FEV1/FVC of 64%, and 20 minutes after inhaled albuterol the FEV1 increases by 16% and 380 mL to 84% of predicted. Based on these diagnostic findings and symptom frequency, which of the following initial drug regimens should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Daily low-dose inhaled corticosteroid with a short-acting beta-agonist as needed
Scheduled long-acting beta-agonist monotherapy without an inhaled corticosteroid
Daily oral systemic corticosteroid therapy with monthly subcutaneous omalizumab
Scheduled nebulized acetylcysteine four times daily with prophylactic antibiotics
q.e: An FEV1 improvement of at least 12–15% (and ≥ 200 mL in adults) after a bronchodilator confirms reversible airway obstruction consistent with asthma. Because symptoms occur more than 2 days per week (persistent asthma), NAEPP Step 2 therapy adds a daily low-dose inhaled corticosteroid controller along with an as-needed short-acting beta-agonist. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 7824–7831, 30454–30487)
q.src: Initiating step-based therapy for newly diagnosed persistent asthma

sections.title: Clinical judgment · Adult trauma

q.q: A 38-year-old man rescued from an apartment fire arrives in the emergency department with facial burns, singed nasal hairs, hoarseness, and coughing of sooty sputum. His initial portable chest radiograph is normal, and his SpO2 is 96% on a nonrebreathing mask. Which of the following diagnostic procedures should the respiratory therapist recommend to evaluate for upper airway injury?
o: Fiberoptic bronchoscopy to directly inspect the airway mucosa
Thoracic computed tomography with intravenous contrast media
Bedside transthoracic ultrasonography of both pleural spaces
Lateral decubitus chest radiography of the dependent hemithorax
q.e: Because initial chest x-rays may be negative and do not detect inhalation injuries, fiberoptic bronchoscopy should be recommended to directly assess airway damage. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 27320–27338)
q.src: Burns/smoke inhalation: fiberoptic bronchoscopy

q.q: A 46-year-old man is intubated and mechanically ventilated on volume-control A/C with PEEP 10 cm H2O after severe blunt trauma caused a massive right-sided pulmonary contusion. Despite optimization of conventional settings, severe refractory shunting persists and blood from the injured right lung is crossing into the uninjured left lung. Which of the following interventions should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Independent lung ventilation via a double-lumen endotracheal tube
High-dose intravenous corticosteroids to reduce contusion edema
External chest wall strapping over the injured right hemithorax
Routine hyperventilation to maintain a PaCO2 below 25 torr
q.e: For patients with a severe unilateral pulmonary contusion when severe shunting persists or cross-over bleeding affects the good lung, independent lung ventilation using a double-lumen endotracheal tube is recommended. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 27027–27045, 20643–20644)
q.src: Chest trauma: independent lung ventilation

q.q: A 29-year-old woman in the trauma ICU with a closed head injury is intubated and mechanically ventilated with a PaCO2 of 37 torr and an SpO2 of 98%. On reassessment, she exhibits extensor posturing, and her right pupil becomes dilated and nonreactive while her intracranial pressure rises to 28 mm Hg. Which of the following pharmacologic interventions should the respiratory therapist recommend immediately?
o: Intravenous mannitol or hypertonic saline to reduce intracranial pressure
High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone to reduce cerebral inflammation
Inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm to increase cerebral vascular blood flow
Nebulized N-acetylcysteine every 4 hours to thin tracheobronchial mucus
q.e: In patients with traumatic brain injury who exhibit posturing and unequal or nonreactive pupils with elevated ICP, osmotherapy with intravenous mannitol or hypertonic saline should be recommended to decrease intracranial pressure. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 27081–27111)
q.src: Head trauma: osmotherapy for acute herniation signs

q.q: A 52-year-old man with 35% body surface area burns and severe smoke inhalation injury is intubated and placed on invasive mechanical ventilation in the burn ICU. He has copious carbonaceous secretions and a high metabolic rate with increased CO2 production. Which of the following ventilator management strategies should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Apply active heated humidification and use a high respiratory rate rather than high tidal volumes
Place a passive heat and moisture exchanger in the circuit and set a high tidal volume of 12 mL/kg
Administer prophylactic systemic corticosteroids and antibiotics to prevent bacterial pneumonia
Maintain a low minute ventilation by setting a respiratory rate of 8/min with a prolonged pause
q.e: Mechanically ventilated burn patients with inhalation injury require active humidification (not an HME) to minimize water loss and tube occlusion, and high minute volumes best achieved via high respiratory rates rather than high tidal volumes. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 27370–27406)
q.src: Smoke inhalation: active humidification and high respiratory rate

sections.title: Clinical judgment · Adult cardiovascular

q.q: A 49-year-old woman in the cardiac ICU with worsening dyspnea and right ventricular enlargement undergoes right-heart pulmonary artery catheterization to differentiate Group I pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) from left ventricular failure. Her cardiac output is 4.0 L/min. Which of the following hemodynamic profiles confirms Group I pulmonary arterial hypertension rather than left ventricular failure?
o: Mean PAP 38 mm Hg, PAWP 10 mm Hg, and PVR 7 mm Hg/L/min
Mean PAP 32 mm Hg, PAWP 24 mm Hg, and PVR 2 mm Hg/L/min
Mean PAP 26 mm Hg, PAWP 22 mm Hg, and PVR 1 mm Hg/L/min
Mean PAP 20 mm Hg, PAWP 12 mm Hg, and PVR 2 mm Hg/L/min
q.e: Pulmonary artery catheterization confirms pulmonary hypertension when mean PAP exceeds 25 mm Hg at rest and differentiates Group I PAH by a normal PAWP (< 15 mm Hg) and high PVR (> 3 mm Hg/L/min), whereas left ventricular failure shows a high PAWP (> 15 mm Hg) and normal PVR. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 27955–27972)
q.src: Pulmonary hypertension: PA catheterization vs LV failure

q.q: A 61-year-old man with hypertension and a 35-pack-year smoking history is evaluated in an outpatient cardiology clinic for substernal chest discomfort that occurs predictably during brisk walking and resolves with rest. His resting 12-lead ECG and chest radiograph in the clinic are normal. Which of the following diagnostic tests should the respiratory therapist recommend next to evaluate for exercise-induced myocardial ischemia?
o: Stress echocardiography or radionuclide myocardial perfusion stress testing
Right-heart catheterization with an inhaled nitric oxide vasodilator trial
High-resolution chest computed tomography without intravenous contrast
Polysomnography with overnight transcutaneous carbon dioxide monitoring
q.e: A normal resting 12-lead ECG does not exclude coronary artery disease; in outpatients with suspected stable angina, stress echocardiography or radionuclide stress testing should be recommended to identify the presence and magnitude of myocardial ischemia. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 27572–27593)
q.src: Outpatient evaluation of stable angina and CAD

q.q: A 64-year-old man presents to the emergency department with crushing substernal chest pain radiating to his left jaw. His 12-lead ECG shows ST-segment elevation in leads V1 through V4, and vital signs are BP 82/50 mm Hg, HR 108/min, RR 24/min, and SpO2 88% on room air. A cardiac catheterization laboratory is available on site. Which of the following management plans should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Give oxygen and aspirin, withhold nitroglycerin and beta-blockers, and arrange percutaneous coronary angioplasty within 90 minutes
Administer sublingual nitroglycerin and intravenous metoprolol immediately, and delay revascularization until troponin labs return
Withhold supplemental oxygen and aspirin, initiate intravenous heparin alone, and schedule an outpatient exercise stress test
Place a pulmonary artery catheter before giving any medications, and start routine intra-aortic balloon counterpulsation
q.e: In STEMI with hypotension (systolic BP < 90 mm Hg), oxygen to keep SpO2 > 90% and aspirin are indicated, whereas nitroglycerin and beta-blockers are contraindicated due to hypotension, and emergency revascularization via percutaneous coronary angioplasty (or CABG) within 90 minutes is recommended. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 27653–27674)
q.src: Acute coronary syndrome: STEMI with hypotension

q.q: A 69-year-old man admitted to the telemetry unit with congestive heart failure has bibasilar crackles, jugular venous distention, and 3+ pitting ankle edema. His blood pressure is 142/86 mm Hg, SpO2 is 93% on 3 L/min nasal cannula, and laboratory results show serum sodium 138 mEq/L and serum potassium 3.1 mEq/L. Which of the following diuretic recommendations is most appropriate for this patient?
o: Recommend a potassium-sparing diuretic such as amiloride instead of furosemide
Administer high-dose intravenous furosemide without any potassium replacement
Withhold diuretic therapy and infuse 2 L of isotonic normal saline over 2 hours
Administer continuous nebulized albuterol to shift potassium into the serum
q.e: Although a loop diuretic such as furosemide is standard for fluid overload in CHF, for a patient needing diuresis who has a low serum potassium (< 3.5 mEq/L), a potassium-sparing diuretic such as amiloride (Midamor) should be recommended instead. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 20538–20544, 20788–20793)
q.src: Decompensated CHF with hypokalemia: diuretic choice

q.q: A 66-year-old man in the surgical ICU develops acute dyspnea and hypoxemia (SpO2 88% on room air, BP 124/76 mm Hg) 2 days after resection of an intracranial brain tumor. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography confirms a right lobar pulmonary embolism, and neurosurgery documents an unacceptably high risk of intracranial hemorrhage that contraindicates systemic anticoagulation. Along with supplemental oxygen to maintain SpO2 at or above 90%, which of the following interventions should be recommended?
o: Placement of an inferior vena cava (IVC) filter to prevent further emboli
Systemic fibrinolytic therapy with an intravenous alteplase infusion
Open surgical pulmonary embolectomy on full cardiopulmonary bypass
High-dose intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion with a bolus
q.e: An inferior vena cava (IVC) filter is indicated for patients with acute pulmonary embolism in whom anticoagulation is contraindicated or when the risk of bleeding is unacceptably high. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 28294–28317)
q.src: Pulmonary embolism with contraindication to anticoagulation

sections.title: Clinical judgment · Adult neurological or neuromuscular

q.q: A 40-year-old man with a catastrophic brain injury is being evaluated for brain death in the ICU. He has no brainstem reflexes, a core temperature of 36.6°C, and a systolic blood pressure of 112 mm Hg without CNS depressants or paralytics. After 10 minutes of preoxygenation on 100% O2 (baseline PaCO2 40 torr, PaO2 240 torr), he is disconnected from the ventilator with 6 L/min O2 via an endotracheal catheter; after 10 minutes no respiratory movements occur and the repeat ABG shows pH 7.19, PaCO2 64 torr, and PaO2 195 torr. How should the respiratory therapist interpret and act on these apnea test results?
o: The test is positive and supports a diagnosis of brain death; reconnect the ventilator and restore original settings
The test is inconclusive because the PaCO2 did not reach 80 torr; extend the disconnection for another 15 minutes
The test is invalid because the SpO2 remained above 85%; repeat the apnea test on room air without supplemental O2
The test excludes brain death because the PaO2 remained above 100 torr; initiate a 30-minute spontaneous breathing trial
q.e: If respiratory movements are absent and the arterial blood gas after 10 minutes shows a PaCO2 of at least 60 torr (> 20 torr rise above baseline), apnea has been demonstrated, which supports a diagnosis of brain death, and the patient should be placed back on the ventilator. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 5478–5497, 7690–7698)
q.src: Brain death determination: apnea test prerequisites and interpretation

q.q: A 45-year-old man with known myasthenia gravis treated with pyridostigmine is admitted to the emergency department with severe weakness, profuse diaphoresis, excessive salivary and bronchial secretions, wheezing, and pinpoint pupils (miosis). When given a diagnostic dose of edrophonium (Tensilon), his muscle weakness acutely worsens. Which of the following medications should the respiratory therapist recommend administering immediately?
o: Atropine to counteract excessive muscarinic acetylcholine activity
Additional intravenous pyridostigmine to improve neuromuscular transmission
Intravenous naloxone to reverse suspected opioid-induced miosis
Oral diltiazem to decrease heart rate and neuromuscular excitability
q.e: A patient with myasthenia gravis who worsens when given edrophonium (Tensilon) and exhibits diaphoresis, bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, and miosis is having a cholinergic crisis from excessive acetylcholine, and atropine is the recommended treatment. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 28480–28512)
q.src: Cholinergic crisis vs myasthenic crisis after Tensilon

q.q: A 50-year-old unimmunized gardener presents to the emergency department 8 days after a deep puncture wound with severe jaw spasms (trismus), neck stiffness, dysphagia, and reflex spasms triggered by light and touch. His upper airway function and ventilation are becoming compromised, and he requires endotracheal intubation and intensive care. In addition to tetanus immunoglobulin and metronidazole, which of the following should the respiratory therapist recommend for intubation and spasm control?
o: Rapid-sequence intubation with succinylcholine and intravenous midazolam for spasms
Awake blind nasotracheal intubation without paralytics and oral pyridostigmine
Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation by full face mask and nebulized albuterol
Immediate tracheostomy under local anesthesia without any sedative medications
q.e: Because intubation in tetanus may trigger severe reflex laryngospasm, rapid-sequence intubation with succinylcholine is recommended when upper airway function and ventilation are compromised, along with an IV benzodiazepine (such as midazolam) to provide sedation and control spasms. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 28655–28671)
q.src: Tetanus airway and spasm management

q.q: A 27-year-old man with a chronic C5 spinal cord injury is evaluated at an outpatient rehabilitation clinic. He breathes spontaneously during the day with a reduced vital capacity, experiences orthostatic dyspnea when sitting upright in his wheelchair, and wants ways to improve his upright breathing efficiency and have brief emergency independence from ventilatory support. Which of the following interventions should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Position an abdominal binder and teach glossopharyngeal (frog) breathing
Apply a tight thoracic rib belt and initiate negative-pressure ventilation
Prescribe continuous supplemental oxygen at 4 L/min via nasal cannula
Perform postural drainage in a head-down Trendelenburg position twice daily
q.e: In the chronic phase of spinal cord injury, an abdominal binder compresses abdominal contents to elevate the diaphragm into a more optimal position for breathing, and patients with an intact upper airway should be taught glossopharyngeal (frog) breathing. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 27265–27280)
q.src: Chronic spinal cord injury: abdominal binder and frog breathing

sections.title: Clinical judgment · Adult medical: infectious disease

q.q: A 55-year-old man who underwent hematopoietic stem cell transplantation 3 weeks ago is admitted to the oncology unit with persistent neutropenia, a temperature of 38.9°C, nonproductive cough, and dyspnea. His SpO2 is 91% on room air, and an initial portable chest radiograph shows no definite focal infiltrate. Which of the following diagnostic imaging studies should the respiratory therapist recommend next to evaluate for an opportunistic pulmonary infection?
o: Computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest
Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) lung scan
Bilateral lower-extremity venous duplex ultrasound
Positron emission tomography (PET) scan of the thorax
q.e: In immunocompromised patients with suspected pulmonary infection, a chest CT scan should be performed early because the pattern of involvement helps establish the etiology and chest CT frequently reveals abnormalities even when the chest radiograph is negative or has subtle findings. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 30097–30118)
q.src: Immunocompromised pulmonary infection: chest CT when CXR is negative

q.q: A 41-year-old man who recently immigrated from a region where tuberculosis is prevalent presents to an outpatient pulmonary clinic with a 4-week history of productive cough, afternoon fevers, night sweats, and a 6-kg weight loss. The clinic physician suspects an active Mycobacterium tuberculosis pulmonary infection. Which of the following microbiological studies should the respiratory therapist recommend to detect active tuberculosis?
o: Serial sputum specimen collection for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stain and culture
A single intradermal Mantoux tuberculin skin test read at 48 to 72 hours
Urinary antigen assays for Legionella pneumophila and Streptococcus pneumoniae
Overnight pulse oximetry with a morning arterial blood gas sample on room air
q.e: While a tuberculin skin test is used to diagnose latent TB infection, serial sputum specimen collection for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stain (along with chest x-ray and IGRA) is recommended to detect an active tuberculosis infection. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 8080–8108)
q.src: Outpatient diagnosis of active vs latent tuberculosis

q.q: A 48-year-old woman is admitted to the medical floor with cavitary right upper lobe infiltrates, hemoptysis, night sweats, and sputum smears positive for acid-fast bacilli, and active pulmonary tuberculosis is strongly suspected. The respiratory therapist is preparing to enter her room to perform a bedside assessment and administer aerosol therapy. Which of the following infection control precautions should be implemented for this patient?
o: Place the patient in a negative-pressure airborne isolation room with the door closed and wear a fit-tested N95 respirator
Place the patient in a standard private hospital room with the door open and wear a surgical mask when within 3 feet of her
Cohort the patient in a semi-private room with a bacterial pneumonia patient and wear clean examination gloves and a gown
Place a surgical mask on the patient inside a positive-pressure isolation room and wear a face shield without a respirator
q.e: Active tuberculosis requires Airborne Precautions, which include placing the patient in a private negative-pressure airborne infection isolation room (AIIR) with the door closed and wearing a NIOSH-certified, fit-tested N95 or higher respirator when entering the room. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 12515–12545)
q.src: Airborne precautions for active pulmonary tuberculosis

q.q: A 67-year-old man with diabetes is admitted to the hospital during winter with acute onset of high fever, myalgias, wheezing, and diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates. A rapid respiratory viral panel from a nasopharyngeal swab is positive for influenza A, and he requires 4 L/min oxygen by nasal cannula to keep his SpO2 at 93%. Which of the following antimicrobial therapies should the respiratory therapist recommend for this patient?
o: Antiviral therapy with oseltamivir (Tamiflu) or zanamivir (Relenza)
Inhaled tobramycin (TOBI) via a breath-enhanced jet nebulizer
Aerosolized pentamidine via a baffled nebulizer with one-way valves
Oral isoniazid and rifampin for a 6-month antimicrobial course
q.e: Viral respiratory infections caused by influenza should be treated with an anti-influenza antiviral agent such as oseltamivir (Tamiflu) or zanamivir (Relenza). (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 20365–20384, 20781–20784)
q.src: Severe influenza pneumonia: antiviral treatment

q.q: A 59-year-old woman with severe bacterial septicemia is intubated and mechanically ventilated in the medical ICU. Her vital signs are stable on PEEP 5 cm H2O and FiO2 0.40, and the ICU team is implementing a ventilator bundle to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP). Which of the following sets of interventions should the respiratory therapist recommend as part of the VAP prevention bundle?
o: Elevate the head of the bed 30 to 45 degrees, perform daily awakening and weaning assessments, and provide regular oral care with chlorhexidine
Keep the patient supine at 0 degrees, replace the ventilator breathing circuit on a 24-hour schedule, and give prophylactic systemic antibiotics
Maintain continuous deep neuromuscular blockade, instill normal saline before suctioning, and change the endotracheal tube on a 7-day schedule
Place a passive heat and moisture exchanger in line with a heated humidifier, and perform routine bronchoalveolar lavage on a 48-hour schedule
q.e: The recommended ventilator bundle for VAP prevention includes elevation of the head of the bed to 30 to 45 degrees, daily awakening trials and assessment of readiness for weaning/extubation, peptic ulcer and DVT prophylaxis, and regular oral care with chlorhexidine. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 29118–29131)
q.src: VAP prevention ventilator bundle

sections.title: Clinical judgment · Adult medical: acute respiratory distress syndrome

q.q: A 61-year-old man is intubated in the ICU after developing acute respiratory distress over 48 hours with no clear-cut predisposing insult. Chest radiograph shows bilateral opacities, and on PEEP 5 cm H2O and FiO2 0.60 his PaO2 is 110 torr. Neck veins are flat and no S3 gallop is heard. Which of the following should the respiratory therapist recommend next to help establish the diagnosis of ARDS?
o: Echocardiography and a plasma BNP level to rule out cardiogenic pulmonary edema
Diagnostic bronchoscopy with biopsy to confirm diffuse alveolar membrane damage
Thoracentesis and pleural fluid analysis to measure the protein and LDH ratios
Helium dilution lung volume testing to quantify the reduction in aerated tissue
q.e: Under the Berlin definition of ARDS, pulmonary edema must not be due to cardiac failure or fluid overload; when there is no clear-cut cause such as aspiration, objective data such as echocardiography and plasma BNP are recommended to rule out hydrostatic/cardiogenic pulmonary edema. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 29154–29190)
q.src: ARDS: ruling out hydrostatic edema

q.q: A 54-year-old woman (height 64 in., predicted body weight 55 kg) with ARDS is ventilated in volume-control A/C at a tidal volume of 275 mL (5 mL/kg PBW), rate 26/min, PEEP 10 cm H2O, and FiO2 0.50. Four hours later her compliance improves and her plateau pressure measures 22 cm H2O. Which of the following ventilator adjustments should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Increase VT by 1 mL/kg until Pplat exceeds 25 cm H2O or VT reaches 6 mL/kg PBW
Decrease VT by 1 mL/kg to a minimum of 4 mL/kg PBW to further lower the Pplat
Keep the current VT of 5 mL/kg PBW and reduce PEEP to 5 cm H2O immediately
Increase VT directly to 8 mL/kg PBW as long as Pplat stays below 35 cm H2O
q.e: Under the ARDSNet plateau pressure guidelines, if Pplat is less than 25 cm H2O and VT is less than 6 mL/kg PBW, VT should be increased by 1 mL/kg until Pplat is greater than 25 cm H2O or VT equals 6 mL/kg PBW. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 21240–21249)
q.src: ARDS: increasing VT when Pplat is below 25 cm H2O

q.q: A 48-year-old man (predicted body weight 70 kg) with severe ARDS is on volume-control A/C with VT 350 mL (5 mL/kg PBW), respiratory rate 35/min, PEEP 14 cm H2O, and FiO2 0.70. Plateau pressure is 29 cm H2O. Arterial blood gas analysis shows pH 7.11, PaCO2 76 torr, and PaO2 64 torr. Which of the following actions should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Increase VT in 1-mL/kg steps until pH exceeds 7.15 and consider NaHCO3
Increase the respiratory rate to 40/min while keeping VT at 5 mL/kg PBW
Decrease VT to 4 mL/kg PBW to keep Pplat below 30 cm H2O and observe
Reduce PEEP to 8 cm H2O to improve CO2 elimination without changing VT
q.e: Under the ARDSNet acid-base guidelines, if the ventilator rate is already at the maximum of 35/min and the pH remains below 7.15, VT should be increased in 1-mL/kg steps until the pH is greater than 7.15 (even if the Pplat target is exceeded) and sodium bicarbonate administration may be considered. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 21250–21259)
q.src: ARDS: severe acidemia (pH < 7.15) at maximum rate

q.q: A 59-year-old woman with severe ARDS is receiving volume-control A/C with PEEP 14 cm H2O and FiO2 0.65. Coarse rhonchi are auscultated over the central airways and the high-pressure alarm sounds intermittently from accumulated secretions. Which of the following should the respiratory therapist do to clear secretions while preventing procedure-associated hypoxemia and loss of PEEP?
o: Preoxygenate with 100% O2 and suction for 10-15 seconds via a closed in-line catheter
Disconnect the circuit and suction for 20-25 seconds after giving three manual breaths
Lower PEEP to 5 cm H2O during open suctioning to avoid barotrauma from the catheter
Instill 10 mL of normal saline down the tube and perform open suctioning for 20 seconds
q.e: In patients receiving invasive ventilatory support for ARDS, ventilator disconnection should be prevented by using an in-line/closed catheter system (or swivel adapter), preoxygenating with 100% O2 for 30-60 seconds, and limiting each suction attempt to no more than 10-15 seconds. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 16701–16717)
q.src: ARDS: preventing suction-induced derecruitment

q.q: A 50-year-old man recovering from ARDS is on volume-control A/C with FiO2 0.40 and PEEP 8 cm H2O, unchanged from yesterday. Systolic BP is 118 mm Hg without vasopressors, neuromuscular blockade was stopped 24 hours ago, and he initiates spontaneous breaths when the ventilator rate is halved for 5 minutes. Which of the following should the respiratory therapist recommend next?
o: Initiate a spontaneous breathing trial on CPAP <= 5 cm H2O with PS < 5 cm H2O and FiO2 < 0.5
Extubate the patient immediately to a high-flow nasal cannula at 40 L/min without a trial
Defer weaning for 24 hours until PEEP is reduced to 0 cm H2O and FiO2 is reduced to 0.21
Switch to synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation at a rate of 10/min with PS 15 cm H2O
q.e: Under the NHLBI ARDS weaning protocol, a patient on FiO2 <= 0.40 and PEEP <= 8 cm H2O (or FiO2 <= 0.50 and PEEP <= 5 cm H2O) at or below the previous day's settings with spontaneous breathing efforts, SBP >= 90 mm Hg without vasopressors, and no neuromuscular blockade should begin a spontaneous breathing trial (up to 120 minutes with FiO2 < 0.5 and PEEP < 5 cm H2O on T-piece, trach collar, or CPAP <= 5 cm H2O with PS < 5 cm H2O). (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 21266–21294)
q.src: ARDS: NHLBI weaning protocol readiness and SBT

sections.title: Clinical judgment · Adult medical: other (immunocompromised, obesity, drug toxicity)

q.q: A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department confused and tachypneic after an intentional ingestion of an unknown liquid found in a garage. Vital signs are HR 118/min, RR 30/min, BP 112/70 mm Hg, and SpO2 97% on room air. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.21, PaCO2 22 torr, PaO2 98 torr, and HCO3 8.5 mEq/L. Which of the following laboratory evaluations should the respiratory therapist recommend to help identify the poisoning?
o: Serum electrolytes to calculate the anion gap and a quantitative toxicology screen
Carboxyhemoglobin measurement by CO-oximetry and a quantitative D-dimer blood test
Plasma brain natriuretic peptide level and serial troponin I cardiac biomarkers
Sputum culture and sensitivity testing with a peripheral white blood cell count
q.e: In suspected poisoning with metabolic acidosis, the respiratory therapist should recommend serum electrolytes and calculation of the anion gap (looking for high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis in salicylate, methanol, and ethylene glycol poisoning) along with a quantitative toxicology screen. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 29299–29318)
q.src: Drug toxicity: lab workup for suspected toxic alcohol or salicylate ingestion

q.q: A 47-year-old man with a BMI of 33 kg/m2 is evaluated at a rural outpatient clinic where polysomnography and portable monitoring are unavailable. Home overnight oximetry is performed and reports an oxygen desaturation index (ODI) of 4/h and a cumulative sleep time with SpO2 below 90% (CT90) of 2%. How should the respiratory therapist interpret this overnight oximetry result?
o: The CT90 below 5% helps rule out sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome
The result confirms severe obstructive sleep apnea needing CPAP
The result diagnoses central sleep apnea from left heart failure
The study is invalid because an overnight CT90 must exceed 15%
q.e: On overnight oximetry, a CT90 (cumulative percentage of overall sleep time with SpO2 < 90%) of less than 5% helps rule out sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (SAHS), whereas an ODI of 15 or more indicates the presence of SAHS. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 29423–29446)
q.src: Obesity and sleep disorders: overnight oximetry CT90 interpretation

q.q: A 42-year-old agricultural worker is admitted to the emergency department with profuse airway secretions, bronchospasm, miosis, bradycardia, and diaphoresis after accidental skin and inhalation exposure to an organophosphate insecticide. His airway is suctioned and supplemental oxygen is applied. Which of the following reversing agents should the respiratory therapist recommend?
o: Atropine and pralidoxime
Flumazenil and glucagon
Naloxone and acetylcysteine
Nitrites and calcium chloride
q.e: Organophosphates (insecticides) cause a cholinergic/parasympathomimetic toxidrome; the specific reversing agents (antidotes) for organophosphate poisoning are atropine and pralidoxime. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 29330–29356)
q.src: Drug toxicity: reversing agent for organophosphate poisoning

q.q: A 29-year-old woman is intubated and mechanically ventilated in the ICU following a life-threatening oral overdose of aspirin (salicylates). Her serum salicylate concentration remains critically elevated with worsening acidemia despite initial gastric decontamination and intravenous fluids. Which of the following systemic interventions should the respiratory therapist recommend to enhance elimination of the drug?
o: Alkaline diuresis via bicarbonate administration and hemodialysis
Intravenous flumazenil administration and continuous glucagon infusion
Endotracheal instillation of naloxone followed by 10 mL of normal saline
Fluid restriction with loop diuretics and high-dose N-acetylcysteine
q.e: In cases of salicylate or barbiturate overdose, alkaline diuresis via bicarbonate administration is recommended, and hemodialysis is recommended for life-threatening ingestions of salicylates, barbiturates, alcohols, amphetamines, and lithium. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 29371–29380)
q.src: Drug toxicity: alkaline diuresis and hemodialysis in severe salicylate overdose

q.q: A 63-year-old man who is immunocompromised on long-term immunosuppressive therapy after a solid-organ transplant is seen in the outpatient pulmonary clinic during autumn. He has no acute respiratory symptoms and asks what preventive measures can reduce his risk of severe pneumonia. Which of the following recommendations should the respiratory therapist make?
o: Immunization with the influenza vaccine and polyvalent pneumococcal vaccine
Daily prophylactic nebulized tobramycin and oral oseltamivir year-round
Routine avoidance of respiratory vaccines while taking immunosuppressants
Weekly bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage to screen for colonization
q.e: High-risk populations, especially immunocompromised individuals, those older than 60 years, the very young, and patients with chronic heart or lung disease, should always be recommended immunization against influenza (flu shot) and S. pneumoniae (polyvalent pneumococcal vaccine). (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 29126–29131, 20373–20382)
q.src: Immunocompromised patient: preventive immunization in clinic

sections.title: Clinical judgment · Adult pre- and post-operative care

q.q: A 49-year-old woman with a body mass index (BMI) of 33.2 kg/m2 is evaluated at an outpatient bariatric surgery clinic. She has no psychiatric disorders or substance abuse and demonstrates commitment to lifestyle changes. Which of the following comorbid findings in her medical record would qualify her as a candidate for bariatric surgery at this BMI?
o: Uncontrollable type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome
Mild intermittent asthma treated with an albuterol MDI
Well-controlled stage 1 hypertension on one medication
Osteoarthritis of the knees with mild joint stiffness
q.e: Adults with a BMI between 30.0 and 34.9 kg/m2 are candidates for bariatric surgery if they have uncontrollable type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome (whereas a BMI of 35.0 to 39.9 kg/m2 qualifies with at least one serious comorbidity, and a BMI >= 40 kg/m2 qualifies without comorbidities). (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 29571–29586)
q.src: Bariatric surgery: candidacy with BMI 30.0-34.9 kg/m2

q.q: A 41-year-old man with a BMI of 44 kg/m2 and a large neck circumference is seen in the preadmission clinic before elective Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. During the L-E-M-O-N airway evaluation, the respiratory therapist asks him to open his mouth fully to determine his Mallampati classification. Which of the following oral inspection findings indicates a Mallampati Class IV airway predicting extreme difficulty with intubation?
o: Visualizing the hard palate without the soft palate or uvula
Visualizing the soft palate, fauces, uvula, and both pillars
Visualizing the soft palate, fauces, and base of the uvula
Visualizing the soft palate and uvula with pillars concealed
q.e: Preoperative bariatric evaluation includes an anesthetic and airway risk assessment because excessive upper airway tissue predisposes obese patients to difficult intubation; on the Mallampati scale, Class IV (able to visualize only the hard palate) predicts extreme difficulty with intubation. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 14015–14027, 14090–14113, 29605–29609)
q.src: Bariatric surgery: preoperative airway risk assessment

q.q: A 64-year-old man is 24 hours status post upper abdominal surgery. He is alert and cooperative, has a dry nonproductive cough with no retained secretions, and has bibasilar atelectasis on chest radiograph. On an FiO2 of 0.40 via air-entrainment mask, his PaO2 is 64 torr (P/F ratio 160), PaCO2 is 37 torr, and pH is 7.41. Which of the following lung expansion therapies should the respiratory therapist recommend as most effective for this patient?
o: Mask CPAP at 5 to 10 cm H2O every 4 to 6 hours for up to 30 minutes
Postural drainage with chest percussion and vibration every 4 hours
Nasotracheal suctioning every 2 hours with nebulized acetylcysteine
Intubation and volume-control ventilation with a PEEP of 12 cm H2O
q.e: Among the various therapies for treating postoperative atelectasis, CPAP (typically 5 to 10 cm H2O every 4 to 6 hours for up to 30 minutes per session) has proven to be the most effective in patients who are hypoxemic (P/F ratio < 300) without retained secretions, decreasing the incidence of intubation and pneumonia. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 16333–16344)
q.src: Postoperative care: CPAP for hypoxemic atelectasis

q.q: A 58-year-old woman is 18 hours status post open cholecystectomy and has coarse rhonchi over both lung fields. When asked to cough, she guards her upper abdominal incision and stops immediately because the explosive exhalation against a closed glottis causes severe pain. Which of the following airway clearance techniques should the respiratory therapist instruct the patient to perform?
o: Forced expiratory technique using two or three huffs with an open glottis followed by rest
Vigorous abdominal thrust coughing with firm epigastric pressure applied over the incision
Sustained maximal inspiration with a 15-second breath-hold followed by an explosive cough
Head-down Trendelenburg postural drainage with manual chest percussion for 30 minutes
q.e: The forced expiratory technique (FET, or huff cough) consists of two or three forced exhalations (huffs) with the glottis open followed by a rest period, and is best suited for postoperative patients for whom explosive exhalation is very painful. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 16173–16180)
q.src: Postoperative care: forced expiratory technique (huff cough)

q.q: Four hours after coronary artery bypass surgery, a 66-year-old man who met all fast-track readiness criteria has been on a spontaneous breathing trial with CPAP 5 cm H2O, pressure support 5 cm H2O, and FiO2 0.40 for 35 minutes. His respiratory rate is 16/min, RSBI is 48, SpO2 is 97%, MAP is 84 mm Hg without vasopressors, and he is alert with an intact cough and no distress. Which of the following actions should the respiratory therapist recommend next?
o: Extubate the patient and prepare to sit him in a chair and initiate deep breathing and coughing
Continue the spontaneous breathing trial for at least 4 hours before considering ETT removal
Return the patient to assist-control ventilation overnight and repeat the trial in the morning
Increase pressure support to 12 cm H2O for 2 hours to rest the muscles before ETT removal
q.e: Under a fast-track cardiac surgery weaning protocol, if the patient remains hemodynamically stable with an acceptable breathing pattern (RSBI < 100) and no signs of distress for at least 30 minutes on pressure support of 5 cm H2O or less, extubation should be recommended, followed as soon as possible by sitting up in a chair, ambulating, and deep breathing and directed coughing. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 27804–27824)
q.src: Cardiac surgery: extubation after 30-minute SBT

sections.title: Clinical judgment · Pediatric

q.q: A 9-year-old boy with persistent asthma returns to the pediatric pulmonary clinic for a routine follow-up visit on a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid. He now reports daytime wheezing 4 days per week, nighttime awakenings 3 times per month, and using his albuterol inhaler 4 days per week. His FEV1 today is 72% of predicted. Before recommending a step-up in his controller therapy, which of the following should the respiratory therapist assess first?
o: Adherence to the drug regimen, inhaler technique, and environmental trigger control
Sputum eosinophil counts, serum total IgE levels, and methacholine challenge results
Arterial blood gas values on room air, chest radiograph findings, and sweat chloride
Peak inspiratory pressure, static lung compliance, and overnight pulse oximetry data
q.e: In a child 5–11 years old, symptoms > 2 days/week, nighttime awakenings ≥ 2/month, SABA use > 2 days/week, and FEV1 of 60–80% predicted indicate asthma that is not well controlled. Before recommending a step-up in the drug regimen, the therapist must first assess compliance with the drug regimen, inhaler technique, and control of environmental factors and coexisting conditions. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 30369–30385, 30496–30501)
q.src: Outpatient asthma control assessment

q.q: A 5-month-old infant born at 29 weeks' gestation with a history of chronic lung disease of prematurity is hospitalized in December for acute viral bronchiolitis. After 3 days of supportive care with nasal suctioning and supplemental oxygen, her respiratory rate is 52/min without retractions, her SpO2 is 94% on room air, and she is taking full oral feedings. As the team prepares this high-risk infant for hospital discharge, which of the following should the respiratory therapist recommend to help prevent severe recurrent respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections?
o: Prophylaxis with the monoclonal antibody palivizumab (Synagis)
Daily maintenance therapy with an inhaled steroid via face mask
Prophylactic aerosolized ribavirin therapy administered weekly
Scheduled oral albuterol syrup given every 6 hours in winter
q.e: Once a hospitalized infant with bronchiolitis meets discharge criteria (respiratory rate < 60–70/min without distress, SpO2 ≥ 92% on room air, and adequate oral feedings), the monoclonal antibody palivizumab (Synagis) should be recommended for prophylaxis against RSV in high-risk infants, including those born prematurely or with chronic lung disease or congenital heart disease. Routine bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and ribavirin are not recommended in bronchiolitis. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 30303–30325)
q.src: Bronchiolitis RSV prophylaxis and management

q.q: A 2-year-old toddler is brought to the emergency department with persistent coughing, tachypnea, dyspnea, and localized wheezing with decreased breath sounds over the right lung field after a sudden choking episode while eating peanuts 3 hours ago. He is alert and in no immediate danger of complete asphyxia, and an anteroposterior chest radiograph shows significant unilateral air trapping on the right with a mediastinal shift to the left. Which of the following should the respiratory therapist recommend to manage this patient?
o: Rigid bronchoscopy under general anesthesia for foreign-body removal
Immediate blind pharyngeal finger sweeps followed by back blows
High-dose nebulized albuterol and intravenous steroids in the ED
Emergency cricothyroidotomy at the bedside before any sedation
q.e: For a child with foreign-body aspiration below the larynx when chest x-rays reveal significant air trapping with a mediastinal shift, rigid bronchoscopy under general anesthesia is recommended to remove the object as soon as possible. Back blows or abdominal thrusts are avoided when the child can cough or speak, blind pharyngeal sweeps are never performed, and cricothyroidotomy is reserved for complete laryngeal obstruction when laryngoscopic retrieval fails. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 30703–30740)
q.src: Foreign-body aspiration management

q.q: A 6-week-old infant born at 27 weeks' gestation (birth weight 980 g) remains intubated in the NICU for severe bronchopulmonary dysplasia and fluid overload, requiring 40% oxygen to maintain an SpO2 of 90%. Current arterial blood gas results on volume-control ventilation show pH 7.26, PaCO2 58 torr, and PaO2 56 torr. Which of the following interventions should the respiratory therapist recommend as part of this infant's care plan?
o: Fluid restriction with hydrochlorothiazide and spironolactone diuresis
Routine high-dose intravenous dexamethasone to reverse lung fibrosis
Immediate transition to high-frequency ventilation with nitric oxide
Increasing the ventilator rate to lower PaCO2 below 35 torr and pH > 7.45
q.e: In infants with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), restricting fluids and providing diuresis using hydrochlorothiazide and spironolactone (not furosemide) may provide benefit, while maintaining volume-control ventilation with permissive hypercapnia (accepting elevated PaCO2 as long as pH > 7.20). Routine systemic corticosteroids (especially dexamethasone), high-frequency ventilation, and inhaled nitric oxide (unless PPHN coexists) are not recommended. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 30824–30855)
q.src: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia ventilator and medical management

sections.title: Clinical judgment · Neonatal: resuscitation

q.q: A 36-week-gestation newborn who required brief stimulation in the delivery room is being observed in the transition nursery 45 minutes after birth. On examination, the respiratory therapist notes seesaw chest and abdominal movement, marked intercostal retractions, just-visible xiphoid retractions, minimal nasal flaring, and expiratory grunting audible with the naked ear. How should the respiratory therapist interpret this infant's Silverman-Anderson score?
o: Score of 8, indicating impending respiratory failure and transfer to intensive care
Score of 4, indicating mild respiratory distress that requires routine nursery care
Score of 2, indicating normal transition after birth with no further intervention
Score of 6, indicating moderate distress that requires a repeat score in 2 hours
q.e: On the Silverman-Anderson index, seesaw movement (2), marked intercostal retractions (2), just-visible xiphoid retractions (1), minimal nasal flaring (1), and expiratory grunting heard with the naked ear (2) sum to a score of 8. A score of 0 indicates no distress, 1 to 6 indicates mild to moderate distress, and a score of 7 or higher indicates impending respiratory failure (any score > 5 after stabilization warrants transfer to intensive care). (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 30985–31005, 31047–31053)
q.src: Silverman-Anderson respiratory distress assessment

q.q: A 33-week preterm newborn in the delivery room was apneic and flaccid at birth and is now 3 minutes old, receiving positive-pressure ventilation via a T-piece resuscitator with a PEEP of 5 cm H2O and an FiO2 of 0.25. Her heart rate has increased to 118/min, and a pulse oximeter sensor on her right hand shows a preductal SpO2 of 73%. Which of the following actions should the respiratory therapist take at this time?
o: Maintain the current FiO2 of 0.25 and continue monitoring preductal SpO2
Increase the FiO2 to 1.00 immediately to raise the preductal SpO2 above 95%
Increase the PEEP to 10 cm H2O and relocate the sensor to the left foot
Initiate chest compressions at a 3:1 ratio and prepare for endotracheal intubation
q.e: For preterm newborns < 35 weeks' gestation, resuscitation begins with low O2 (21–30%) titrated to targeted preductal SpO2 (right hand) by time after birth: 60–65% at 1 minute, 65–70% at 2 minutes, 70–75% at 3 minutes, 75–80% at 4 minutes, 80–85% at 5 minutes, and 85–95% at 10 minutes. Because a preductal SpO2 of 73% at 3 minutes is within the 70–75% target range and the heart rate exceeds 100/min with PEEP ≤ 5 cm H2O, the current FiO2 should be maintained. (Heuer & Rodriguez 4th ed., lines 21635–21667, 31015–31032)
q.src: Delivery room preductal SpO2 titration

q.q: A 30-week-gestation newborn (3 days old) in the NICU on a 28% oxyhood is receiving daily caffeine and continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring for apnea of prematurity. The apnea alarm sounds; the infant is acyanotic with a heart rate of 108/min, but the apnea does not self-correct after 10 seconds, and tickling the feet, briefly suctioning the oropharynx, repeating tactile stimulation, and slightly extending the neck all fail to restore breathing. Which of the following should the respiratory therapist do next?
o: Apply bag-and-mask ventilation using 28% oxygen (the pre-episode FiO2)
Apply bag-and-mask ventilation using 100% oxygen for 2 minutes
Begin chest compressions at a 3:1 ratio and administer IV epinephrine
Perform immediate endotracheal intubation and initiate HFOV at 15 Hz
